apprehension exists as to the object and effect
of the Bill which, in common with Mr. H.

of the Criminal Law Amendment Act of last
Session, it may perhaps be useful if I address
to you scimo observations in explanation of it.
The history of my connection with the
question is very simple. Beyond the fact that
I voted against the Lords' amendments in the
Bill of last year, I had not taken any active
part in the matter. Early in the present
Session Mr. HOWELL and Mr. N.ACDONALD
called upon me, and requested me to under-
take the amendment of the present Act.
Feeling the difficulty of a question in which
such large interests are involved and such
strong feelings are enlisted on either side, I
told these gentlemen I could not move in the
matter unitise I was satisfied, by a careful
study of the proceedings which had taken
place, that some actual miscarriage of justice
had arisen under the Act. Unless that was
the ease, I knew it would be idle even to
attempt to alter legislation of so recent
a date. On being furnished by Messr3.
HOWELL and MAcnowiLD with a report of the
eases which had been adjudged, I came to the
conclusion that the law had been in some
instanies erroneously interpreted, and there-
fore wrongly administered—especially in the
Bolton and Hammersmith cases—and that
great practical injustice had occurred. It
appearcd to me that this miscarriage had
arisen from the confused manner in which the
Act was drawn, which involved the whole
subject-matter in obscurity ; and I also
observed that tho practical evils complained
of wore confined almost exclusively to decisions
in respect of the offence known as " picket-
ting,” under the "watching and besetting"
section of the Act.

Being satisfied that there was a practical
evil, and believing that the gentlemen who
applied to me had authority from those in.
terested in the matter to request me to deal

and extent of the amendments proposed in the

This is the substantial amendment proposed
in the Act of 1871. I belive it is in conformity
with the real intention of that Act, though the

confusion, and, therefore, to injustice in
its administration.

For though the view of some of tire magis-
trates that simple " picketting " is an offence
under the Act of 1871, has never been upheld
on appeal—the Bolton decision having been
overruled, and that in the Hammersmith case
having been abandoned—yet the fact of the
conviction has worked great hardship and in-
justice.
It having been thought necessary to re-
move all room for doubt on this point in the
manner I have stated, we also thought it
advisable to re-arrange in a more lucid and
logical form—without substantial alteration—
the complicated language of the rest of the
section. This has been effected with his usual
skill by Mr. Wafoirr, the draftsman of the Bill.
This is substantially what we propose to do
from the point of view and with the objects I
have stated, it is for those who are interested
in the matter to determine whether it is an
end which they care to see accomplished.
I observe that there are some persons who
declare their determination to be satisfied with
nothing short of the total repeal of the Act of
1871. I would venture to point out to them
that such a repeal would not effect their pur.
pose, for it would destroy the statutory legali-
sation of the right of combination. And if
those who demand such a repeal require that
no prohibition against overt nets of violence,
intimidation, and molestation, in furtherance
of such combination, shall be enacted, I have
already said I cannot concur in such a proposal.
I know it is urged that such legislation is
unjust because it is special. The objection
appears to me more plausible than sound. A
great part of our legislation is and always
must be special, in order to meet special evils
and special circumstances. The Factory Acts,
which limited the hours of labour, were special
Acts to remedy special evils. The Mines
Regulation Bill and the Truck Bill will be
special legislation to deal with special cases.
To say that no laws shall be passed which are
not universal in their application, is to exhibit
a want of acquaintance with the conditions of
practical statesmanship. That there have
been, and may be again, special evils connected
with the action of Trades Unions, is a thing
which it would be in vain to deny. The real
question is, what are the matters in respect of
such combinations against which it is right,
and what are those against which it is not
right, to legislate.

Now our Bill, though in form a re-enacting
measure, is in substance (and it is to the sub-
stance not to the form that practical minds
will look) a 13111 partly of repeal, partly of re-
arrangement of the Act of 1871. If it were
passed it would leave the law substantially as
follows :

I have always thought that the only prin-
ciple on which the apparently conflicting, but
really identical, interests of capital and labour
can be reconciled, is by the assertion and
maintenance of the rights of both parties to
deal with the commodity which either has to
dispose of with the most absolute freedom ; that
the employer should deal in his wages and the
workman in his labour in such manner and on
what terms ho pleases. To this freedom is
inherent the right of combination on either
side—a right which is admitted in trade of all
descriptions, and the trade in labour differs in
no respect from that in any other article of
commerce.

Now the advantage to the workmen of the
Act of last Session was that it did deliberately
recognise this right of combination, which it is
well known had been previously disallowed by
the common law doctrine against restriction
upon trade. It was thought proper, and in my

freedom of individual action on the part of those
who did not think fit to take part in it. The
Legislature ought not, and certainly would
not have allowed it to he supposed that
whilst combination was authorised, coercion,
either by violence, intimidation, or molesta-

punished. On the other hand, the framers of

" picketting," if confined to more watching

is only noxious when accompanied
by overt acts of violence, annoyance, or
menace. Now it appeared to us that tho

Act of 1871 lent itself to the former

mon cannot be led into Conservatism, let thorn

ing for nothing in the State. Why should

lutely necessary that trades unionists should

swoon? The Cartrum and Mexrikaim when

Cause them to lose the advantageous position they

THE STONEMASONS.

On Saturday a large meeting of the operative
masons who have been locked out was held in the
Sun Concert-hall, Mason-street, Westminster-road.
Mr. Broadhurst took the chair, and in opening the
proceedings congratulated the meeting upon the
prompt manner in which their brother masons
working for Mr. Brass and Messrs. Jackson and
Shaw bad responded to the call made upon them
by the general meeting of the trade. Not a man
out of the whole number had stopped in; both
society and non-society men had acted with the
most praiseworthy unanimity. The works of the
new Colonial Office, the new Post Office, Burling.
ton House, and the Midland Railway Hotel were
now at a complete standstill.

The meeting then proceeded to arrange the
details for conducting the lock-out in the masons'
branch of the trade, which was done in a practical
and business-like manner. The masons, baying
appointed a Lock-out Committee, gave that cotn-.
mittee their confidence, leaving it to manage all
those numerous details which can only be satisfac-
torily dealt with by a small body. Among the
business done at the above meeting was the
strengthening of the Lock-out Committee by
adding to it the names of Messrs. Broadhurst and
Gray. This Committee.now consists of seven,
with a treasurer and secretary. The meeting then
proceeded to consider financial business, and it
was unanimously resolved that, in case it was re-
quisite for the masons to make any appeal to other
trades for pecuniary support, that appeal should
be made independently of the other branches of
the building trade, their course having been found
to work most satisfactorily to all parties during the
former lock-out. It was also resolved to recom-
mend to the committee to cordially co•operate
with all other lock-out committees formed by the
men in the other branches of the trade. The
meeting was then adjourned.

The masons held another meeting on Monday
morning, Mr. Harrison, a central committeeman,
in the chair. The business transacted was quietly
and quickly disposed of. Masons, from the very
nature of their trade, have always been a migra-
tory body, and the statement may be relied upon
that lots of these men were away searching for
work in the provinces. Nevertheless, the number
left behind is more than sufficiently largo, and a
resolution was confirmed, earnestly appealing to
the Manchester masons for pecuniary help, with a
rider added, that should they over be reduced to
the same straits, the London masons would not
forget the obligation. While this matter WAR
under consideration, some complaints were made
that the papers had mule it appear the masons
only contemplated asking for external assistance,
"should it become necessary," whereas the reso-
lution announced from the chair on Saturday
directly affirmed it was requisite, and that the
papers and books were being printed to enshle the
appeal to be made. It was stated that no dividend
could be made till the close of the week, and,
apropos of this question, a suggestion was thrown
out by a society man, to the evident satisfaction
of the bulk of the meeting, that non-society men,
in this crisis, were entitled to the generous consi-
deration of the committee. The Chairman was
sure the matter might be safely left in the hands
of the Committee, who would hereafter bring up a
proposal on the subject.
A meeting of the locked out masons was held on
Tuesday morning at the Sun Concert-hall, West-
minster-road, when several resolutions were dis-
cussed and adopted in reference to the lock-cut.
Reports were delivered in as to the pmeeeilings
going on at some of the firms who have not locked
out to thwart the movement, and delegates were
appointed to investigate them, with the power, if

true, to call the men out at once. The chairman
in addressing the meeting on the position of affairs,
spoke of the question of arbitration. He said he
did not agree in submitting trade questions to
persons who could not thoroughly understand
them. lie believed that if four men and four
employers were to meet together with an honest
desire to settle the dispute, they could do so in
half an hour. They wanted no outside arbitrators.
The committee reported that large numbers of the
younger men were daily leaving for the country.
Mr. Broadhurst and Mr. Weighill, who have
been to Manchester on deputation, reported the
result •of their visit. They bad waited upon the
secretaries of all the large trades in the district,
by whom they had been most cordially received.
Having fully explained the position of the lock-
out in London, they had received distinct promises
of pecuniary support. A large aggregate meet-
ing of the Manchester trades would be held in a
few days. They had also visited the various
masons' lodges in Manchester, from whom efficient
support might be expected. The report was
received with much satisfaction, and a vote of
thanks was given to the deputation.
On Wednesday morning the deputation from
the Trades Council, consisting of Mr. King, book-
binder; Mr. Wood, ironfounder ; and Mr.
Morgan, waited upon the mason's lock -out
committee, sitting at the Sun Tavern, Westmin-
ster-road, and laid before them the resolution of
the Council, stating the reasons why it had been
adopted. The deputation was courteously received
by the committee, who informed them that they
did not look upon the resolution with any
favour, nor did they think it was likely to find
favour with the men. The committee further
informed the deputation that they had been given
to understand that the masters NI ould rather con -
cede tho extra wages asked than give the nine
hours.

An aggregate meeting of the masons of London
was held last night to consider the steps to be
adopted to carry out the strike threatened or con-
templated on the Ist of July, unless the demands
of their memorial were complied with. At the
beginning of the year notice was given to the
masters that "the masons in London and its
vicinity are desirous of continuing the nine
hours system all the year round, instead
of only between the 9th November and 14th
February; and that on and after the Ist
July next the wages be 9d. an hour, making the
average weekly wages for nino as near as possible
that hitherto received for ten hours per day." It
was decided to wait the result of the luck-out
before resorting to the extreme measure said to
have been looked forward to for some time pas t.

articles.title: PAINTERS.
articles.text:
THE PAINTERS.

On Wednesday night an aggregate meeting of
the operative house painters and decorators, to
consider their position in reference to the existing
lock-out in the building trade, was held in Cam-
bridge-hall, Newman-street, Oxford-street. Mr.
Shipton occupied the chair.
The Chairman explained that the meeting had
been convened by a committee of delegates, re-
presenting the various local societies and the
principal firms in the metropolis, to ascertain
whether the trade as a body wore prepared to
support the movement for the nine hours, and, if
so, to adopt it memorial to the masters requesting
them to grant the nine hours per day, or 51 hours
per week. It was very fortunate that this com-
mittee of delegates was in existence, as by that
organization they would be able to raise subscrip-
tions for the support of those painters who were
now out of employment owing to the lock-out.
Ile quite endorsed the action taken by the carpen-
ters and masons, and hoped they would receive the
undivided support of the trades at large.
Mr. Salter then moved the following resolu-

articles.text:
tion :

That this meatiux authorize the committee of
delegates to memorialise the masters to concede
nine hours as a working day for the first five days
of the week, and six on the Saturday, making a
total of 51 hours per week.

Mr. Phillips seconded the resolution, and said
the trade would not rest until they bad obtained
the nine hours.

Professor Beesly supported the resolution, and
in so doing traced the rapid growth of Trade
Unionism within the last few years. In reference
to the present dispute in the building trade, he
defended the action taken by the masons and car-
penters, and said the offer of arbitration made by
the master builders was a gross insult to the work-
men, and the men were justified in refusing it
upon the terms offered. Whether they should
accept arbitration upon any other terms was a
question for the men thenrselv&a to determine.
If they had faith in the justice of their demand,
and fat thetuaelves stroug enough to obtttin it,

JUNE 28, 1872.

then it was not likely they would agree to accept
arbitration, which almost always ended in a com-
promise. He was glad to hear from the men that
they looked upon the nine hours as more important
than the wages.

Mr. Frederic Harrison also supported the reso-
lution, following the same line of argument as the
previous speaker. He entered very fully into the
question of arbitration, and contended that no
arbitration could be permanent and satisfactory'
unless the Board of Arbitration was formed of an
equal number of masters and men.
The resolution was carried unanimously.
Mr. Myerson moved the second resolution as
follows :

That the memorial to the employers also contain
a request that the future minimum rate of wages
fr house painters be Sid. per hour, leaving the
maximum wages to be fixed by mutual agreement'
between the workman and his employer."
Mr. Gohagan seconded the reso!ution, which
was supported by Professor Levy, and also carried
unanimously.

It was resolved that the employers be requested
to appoint a committee of their body to confer with
an equal number of workmen for the purpose o
drawing up a code of working rules.

articles.title: FITTERS AND SMITHS.
articles.text:
THE FITTERS AND SMITHS.

On Tuesday night, at the Cambridge Hall,
Newman-street, there was a meeting of the
builders' smiths and ironworkers. These men
have had till now no union, and the unionists
among them have been only the few who joined
the Amalgamated Society of Engineers. The
lock-out has speedily taught them the necessity
of learning to stand on their own bottom. When
the smiths got locked out they had nowhere to
turn, till two or three of the craft improvised a
committee, and convoked a general meeting of the
trade. The summons was issued from Rose-street,
Soho, where a provisional administration has been
in power for several days. It drew together a
large assemblage in the Cambridge Hall, and the
preliminary business of organization was carried
through with order and energy. When the
objects and causes of the separate movement bad
been explained by a number of speakers, a com-
mittee was elected, to consist of the following
members from the leading shops in London :
Tuthill (W. Cubitt and Co.), Vivian (Smith and
Taylor), Halford (Dines and Co.), Baker (Trollops
and Sons), Fleming (Freakes), Lindon (Myers),
Edwards (Jackson and Shaw), Wright (Aldins).
These men, acting as a supervising committee,
will meet daily at the Rose and Crown, in Soho.
In addition to the committee, fourteen delegates
for shops and jobs were appointed from among
those present at the meeting. As soon as unrepre-
sented shops are apprised of such action, they will
no doubt hasten to pltee themselves in communi-
cation with the central committee. The promoters
of the smiths' delegation desire to create a distinct
fund, and to receive for the benefit of their own
members the subscriptions of their trades. They
hold in view as an ultimate desideratum the
foundation of an amalgamated society of smiths
and ironworkers.

articles.title: PLASTERERS.
articles.text:
THE PLASTERERS.

The plasterers held a general meeting of the
trade on Thursday evening, at the Agricultural
Hall, Llington, for the purpose of appointing
a committee to co-operate with the other branches,
and arranging the details for raising a fund to
support the men locked out. The plasterers for
several years have been without any organization,
and. now they find themselves in a very unsatis-
factory position.

articles.title: LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE LABOURERS.

The locked-out labourers intend holding a general
mooting this evening (Friday) in Trafalgar.square
for the purpose of appealing to public sympathy.
These moa have not taken any part in the move-
ment through which they have been thrown
out of employment. They have no society to fall
back upon, and their case is one of great hard-
ship. It Li to be hoped that a good committee will
be got together, and that an appeal will be made
to the tradesmen on their behalf.

FRIDAY.—The labourers have issued the follow-
ing address: —We respectfully request your aid in
making known our present position to the public.
The leek-out in the building trade has thrown
out of employ 5,000 labourers who were dependent
upon their scanty earnings for a living. Although
we are in no way responsible for the dispute, WO
are the greatest sufferers by it, as we have no union
to support us. We have culled upon the carpenters
and ma:ons for the purpose of finding out whether
they would assist us in any way, but they could
not promiso any help. The empleyols are raising
a guarantee fund 011500,000, by making a levy of
6d. for each man ill their employ on the 7th of

June, such fund to compensate the smaller mem-
bers of their trade society for any loss they may
sustain through taking part in the lockout. The
carpenters and masons have large funds, but we
have no resource but to appeal to the general
public; and many of the labourers locked out
would willingly leave London if they had the
means and could hear of a chance to get w ork.
Our treasurer is Samuel Taylor, Esq., President
of the Working Man's Club and Institute, 61,
Broadwall, Lambeth, to whom all Post Office
Orders can be made payable at the Post Office,
Blackfriars-road.

JAMES lIALLonas, Labourer,
Secretary of Labourers' Locked-out Committee.
London General Labourers' Lock-out Com-
mittee, 51, Broadwall, Lambeth, June 26.

articles.title: MEETING OF THE MASTERS.
articles.text:
MEETING OF THE MASTERS.

The Executive Committee of the Central Asso-
ciation of Master Builders assembled on Monday
at the Freemasons' Tavern for routine business
purposes, and "taking stock" of the first week's
lock-out. It is stated that they saw no reason to be
discouraged, or to weaken the determination they
bad previously come to. Ample assurances of
public sympathy were being tendered daily, and
it is certain the official list of lock-outs will show
a larger total on every occasion of its issue. It is
estimated by the masters that the number of men
already out approaches very nearly that of 1859.
Should this prove to be correct, it will furnish ad-
ditional evidence of the great expansion of the
building trade of London during the past thirteen
years, and demonstrate the amount of disturbance
now going on in this important branch of Metro-
politan industry. The "partial" lock•outs admit
of a simple explanation. The men retained are
not workmen in the ordinary sense, paid by the
hour, but attached to the establishment all the
year round, receiving weekly wages, no matter
whether they work or not. Frequently, in slack
times, they have nothing whatever to do, but are
yet paid all the same, and the masters solemnly
affirm that, with these justifiable exceptions, every
lock-out has been, and still remains, real and Lona
fiefe. One of the resolutions adopted by the com-
mittee was that every master builder be called upon
to pay the sum
.of 6d. per head for every man he had
in his employ on the 7th of June, and this resolu-
tion was embodied in a circular and sent round to
the trade. The money thus raised will go to form a
guarantee fund out of which to compensate those
masters who may suffer special pecuniary loss
from locking-out. Another printed document has
been sent to those employers who have not locked
out, for presentation to their men to sign, of which
the following is a copy :

"I hereby engage with Messrs, --- not to
contribute any money, directly or indirectly, to
support those men who are now on strike, or who
are looked out through the demands of the Trades'
Union." •

A meeting of Master Painters and Decorators
was held at the West End on Tuesday night.
There were over thirty-five gentlemen present, all
of whom joined the Masters' Association, and gave
their ready assent to this resolution, viz., " That
this meeting of decorators and jobbing builders in
the west and north-west district of London do
hereby resolve to bind themselves not to corn-
menu) or undertake on any pretext whatever any
fresh jobs or work until the question between the
men now on strike and the Master Builders' Asso-
ciation be satisfactorily settled, daily jobbing re-
quirements excepted.

articles.title: EXTENT OF THE LOCK-OUT.
articles.text:
EXTENT OF THE LOCK-OUT.

The various Look-out Committees have received
returns of, the number of men locked out, and
though these returns are far from being complete,
they are sufficient to form something like an ap-
proximate estimate of the total number of men
locked out, which appears less than has been
stated. From these returns it would ap-
pear the numbers are as follows : —7Citt penters
and joiners, about 2,600; masons, 800; brick-
layers, 300; plasterers, 300 ; painters, GOO ;
smiths, l 50; plumbers, &c., shout 500. It is
probable that when the returns are complete this
number will he increased. The comparatively
small number of bricklayers and plasterers arises,
us stated by the Committee, from the fact that a
considerable number of the out-door jobs of the
locking-out masters, upon which those classes of
workmen are alone employed, have not been sus-
pended. Ni) one passing about the mAropolis and
seeing the large amount of building operations
going on would suppose that there was a lock-out
existing in the building trade. The closed gates of
the building yams of some of the large firms are,
however, outward signs of the lalnontLblo state
4fEtirs (Aisting.

articles.title: ACTION OF THE LONDON TRADES COUNCIL.
articles.text:
ACTION OF THE LONDON TRADES
COUNCIL.

A meeting of the delegates of the London trades,
forming the London Trades' Council, was held on
Tuesday night at the Bell Inn, Old Bailey; Mr.
Odger in the chair.

Messrs. Smith and Wright attended as a deputa-
tion from the Central Committee of Carpenters to
explain to the Council the position of the present
lock-out and strike in the building trade, and to
solicit the support of the Council. The deputation
having addressed the meeting, considerable discus-
sion ensued, in which a general feeling was ex •
pressed that some attempt should be made by the
Council to effect an amicable settlement.

Mr. Coulson, bricklayer, then moved the follow-
ing resolution
"That in the opinion of this meeting the country
generally has accepted nine hours as the future
working day for all trades. Therefore, the opera-
tives in the building trades are quite right in
seeking to ensure the nine hours, and are deserving
the sympathy and material support of all trade
societies; but this meeting deems it to be its duty
to advise the men locked out to submit the follow-
ing proposition to their employers :—‘ That the
nine hours be conceded and commenced on a given
day, that the men return to work immediately on
the nine hours being agreed to, that the question
of wages and the code of working rules be arranged
by a board of arbitration, consisting of an equal
number of masters and men, whose decision &mil
be final.' "

Mr. Monteith, cooper, seconded the resolution.

A long discussion ensued, in which it was dis-
tinctly stated that should the men locked out
doclino to accede to the above resolution, the
support of the trades would still be accorded to
them.

Upon the resolution being submitted, it was
carried.

A deputation of three delegates was then ap-
pointed to convoy the above resolution to the
masons' and carpenters' meeting.

articles.title: LONDON UNITED SOCIETY OF CHAIR MAKERS AND CARVERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON UNITED SOCIETY OF
CHAIR MAKERS AND CARVERS.

A meeting of this trade was held on Wednesday
evening at the Old Axe Tavern, Hackney-road, to
consider the state of the trade. A deputation
from the Trade Council spoke on trade organiza-
tion, the short time movement, and the Criminal
Law Amendment Act.

Mr. G. Hay occupied the chair.
The Chairman stated the objects of the meeting,
and that all should assist.

Mr. Titchuo said he was there to advocate tho
cause of combination. He asked them to assist
themselves and follow the example of the carpenters
and others. As the weekly subscription was small
he thought all should respond and join who thought
themselves fit.

A delegate from the London Trades Council
then addressed the meeting.
The cabinet makers' delegate said: We only
ask you to do that which we have done
ourselves ; join, and you can command a fairer
'nice. If we are members the masters do not put
the screw on if they know that you can protect
yourselves. We have 1,300 members in our so-
ciety. If all join, trades will be on a level.

Mr. Annerne said that Mr. Lueraft allowed un-
asked 51 hours fur the week. He hoped they would
have the support of this establishment.
Mr. Oliver said they ought to protect themselves
against masters, and to protect themselves against
each other.

Mr. F. Allen said it was decided at a cabinet
maker's shop meeting that the men should have
time and half-time fur overtime. The master said,
lot other shops do the same, as it was a question
between capital and ltbour.

The Tirades' Council delegate said that picket-
ting should be legal, as they only wanted to
know the condition of the shop so as to reguhte
their funds. The masters say you want to intimi-
date. He did not believe it. The Criminal Law
Amendment Act came down from the House of
Lords rendering picketting illegal, so that if you
unknowingly approach a shop you may be accused.
But, workmen, speak your minds.

It was resolved and carried
"That the society was worthy of the support of
the trade and those-eonneof ed with it."

2. That the rapid strides machinery has made
in reducing the necessity of intellectual and
physical labour requires more time for labour to
protect itself to compete successfully with the long
hours of labour, so deteriorating to the physical
condition of the labourer ; and that the short timw.
movement is worthy of your support.
3. That this meeting considers the Criminal Law
Amendment Act an ujust attempt to interfere
with the legitimate right of combination on the
part of labour, and this 'netting pledges itself to
support its repeal.

articles.title: RAILWAY SERVANTS. •
articles.text:
THE RAILWAY SERVANTS. •

A new "service" has been added to the number
of official castes which govern the country. The
railway employ6s, from being a horde of casuals,
have suddenly changed into a powerful organiza
tion. It is barely a year since Mr. Bass, by his
tilt with the Midland Railway directors, enlisted
public sympathy on behalf of over-worked guards,
engine drivers, and signal-men. When that con-
troversy subsided, he did his prottigos a still more
substantial benefit by teaching them self-help
He advised them to combine for mutual protection,
and liberally supplied the means of drawing them
together, and making railway servants as a body
better acquainted with each other. The organiza-
tion has thriven on an infant diet of memorials
and remonstrances, hardly one of which failed to
secure some concession from directors.
.It con-
voked a conference in London for the framing of
a constitution. Several hundreds of delegates re-
presenting all the principal railway centres of
England have been employed on that task for three
days past, and on Wednesday they brought it to a
most satisfactory and harmonious conclusion.

On Wednesday night they held a public meeting
in the Arundel Hall, more for the sake of ex-
pressing their gratitude to. the Members of Par-
liament who befriended them in their early
struggles. The hall vim packed from the hack
door to the front of the platform. The majority
were num who could evidently see as straight be-
fore thorn, in an argument or a matter of princip!o,
as they could on the footboard of a locomotive.
They seemed proud of their legislative guests.
When Mr. Bass, M.P., Mr. Morley, M.P., Mr.
Straight, M.P., Canon Jenkins, Mr. Lloyd-
Jones, Mr. Vincent, Mr. G. Potter, and the chief
delegates entered the room, every man started to
his feet and cheered lustily, till the procession
had reached the platform. The Lime intense
appreciative spirit infused itself into all the pro-
ceedings.

Mr. Samuel Morley, M.P., presided, and in
opening the proceedings stated that he cordially
concurred in the object which the society had in
view. It had not been formed out of any hostility
to railway directors or companies, but simply as a
means of enabling the men to unite in considering
their condition and circumstances, and to, bring
what demands they might consider it necessary to
make before the proper authorities in a united
'body. Ho ,was a large employer of labour him self
and he saw no reason why there should be any
Antagonism between the employer and the em-
ployed. To his mind the interests of both were
identical. The men employed on railwaye were
differently situated from all other classes, and upon
their attention and good conduct the safety of the
public depended. It was, therefore, the interest
of the public to see that they were not worked. so
as to make it physically impossible for them to at-
tend to those duties; and whea a man was
worked sixteen hours a day, as he had heard of some
railway men being, it was impossible that such a
man could properly attend to his work or duties.
He therefore cordially concurred in the object the
men in this ease had in view, and if they prose-
cuted their object with respect, moderation, and
consideration, he was sure they would. have the
sympathy and the support of the public. (Leud
cheers.)

Mr. Baxter Langley, on behalf of the railway
servants, then presented Mr. Bass, ALP., with the
following address:—

-"Resew= Stu,—Wo, the undusigned dele-
gates, in meeting, assembled, and represamting
the members of the Amalgamated Society of

to you our deep and heartfelt gratitude . for, your
sympathy. for the .sufferings endured by the Mass
to which we belong, and for the timely support
and invaluable aid rendered by you in the forma-
tion of the society, which we trust may bathe
instrument of improving our social condition,
protecting our rights, and guarding us against
. -

-"
The universal respect and esteem of railway
servants throughout the kingdom will always be
yours, and your name. will be cherished Amongst
them as a household word, and enshrined on. their
grateful memories. We, therefere, trust that you
will allow us to inscribe that honoured name as
the patron of . the Association which owes its

THE TURNERS' SOCIETY.

On Tumidity night the regular weekly meeting
of the Clerkenwell Branch of the Amalgamated
Turners' Mutual Aid Society, was held at their
meeting house, the Crown and Can, St. John's-
etreet, Clerkenwell.
After several important questions affecting the
general interest of the trade were discussed,
The General Secretary, Mr. Dixon, reported
progress of -the week. lie said ke was glad to be
able to tell them the General Turners' Society had
amalgamated with them; that he had also estab-
lished another branch at the East-end of London,
which now made four branches in London. He
was happy to tell them they had no one on the
funds of the Union at present, and trade being
good he thought there was no fear of any. There
were at the present time 2,000 members in the
union; that distrieti had been formed all over the

members were joining from all parts of London
daily.

at the Crown 4nd Can, at half-past eight on

ing a General Committee for London."

closed the meeting.

THE LONDON TRADES COUNCIL
AND THE CRIMINAL LAW
AMENDMENT ACT.

A meeting of the London trades, forming the
London Trades Council, was held on Wednesday
night, at the Bell Inn, Old Bailey, for the purpose
of receiving a report from the Executive Committee
on the Bill now before Parliament, introduced bY
Mr. Vernon Harcourt, for the amendment of the
Criminal Law Amendment Act. Nearly
all the
principal trades were represented. Mr. Odger
occupied the chair, and briefly opened the pro-
ceedings.
Mr. Shipton, the secretary, read the report
of the committee, as fullows :—" We have fully
considered the Bill, introduced into the House of
Commons by Mr. Harcourt, to amend the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, and we regret to
say that all the advantages which it would confer,
if passed into law, would be obtained by a much
shorter method, by simply moving the omission
of the words relating to watching and besetting
from the Act itself. If the Bill in question
becomes law it would still retain some of the
worst features of the Act itself. Under these cir-
cumstances, therefore, we cannot accept nor adept
the Bill introduced by Mr. Harcourt as a eottle-
ment of the question, and we earnestly urge
the London trades to hold a great demonstration
to request the absolute repeal of the Act."
After a short discussion the report was unani-
mously adopted, and it was afterwards resolVed
that the demonstration should be an open air
demonstration, and a committee was appointed to
carry out the details.

The joiners and carpenters of Lincoln have ad-

Ist of January, 1872, they issued circulars to
the master builders, giving them to understand that

Present rate of wages, making them 61. per hour

Meetings of the masters' committee and the depu-

had presided over the !meetings, which was carried
unanimously.

the terms agreed to by the masters' committee
and the deputation, all appearing thankful that

FRIDAY, JUNE 28, 1872.

THE CARPENTERS' AND JOINERS'
LOCK-OUT.

THE working men of England never took
anything in hand more important than the
nine hours movement. The employers under-
stood this from the first, as may be seen from.
Sir Wm. ARMSTRONG'S letter to the Tunes, ill
which he stated that time once granted could
never be taken back. We say it is important,
because it includes everything else. It is not
only rest, comfort, enjoyment, health, and im-
provement of the mind, but it is a permanently
depleted labour market, and means, in conse-
quence, a higher price for labour, and an in-
crease of personal independence to the worker.
To secure this every energy should be
strained; every legitimate device employed;
and, above all, everything should be done
with caution, prudence, and skilfulness, so
that a cause so good should not suffer injury

through incompleteness of thought or rashness
of action. It is true this movement has been
thoroughly successful so far. But those who
are interested in it, and who are called on to
take part in it, should not look on past success
as guaranteeing the future. Every now
struggle should be entered on with as
much forethought and caution as if no-
thing had been won, inasmuch as one
important defeat might roll back in a
most disastrous manner the tide of victory,
and force upon the men, under circumstances
perhaps far less favourable than the present,
the necessity of reconquering their lost ground,
and completing their victory through incal-
culable loss, delay, and suffering.
We desire to avoid saying a word or sug-
gesting a thought that might cause even the
slightest division in the ranks of the men;
but what we have to say is better spoken now
than at any other time. And that it should
be spoken out in the interest of the men wo
cannot have a moment's doubt. It would be
out of place now to raise any question as to
the prudence of asking "all in a lump," as it
were, for shorter time, higher wages, and im-
provement in the code which regulates con-
ditions of work. Whether so complicated a
demand was prudent is a question the men
themselves will have opportunity of consider-
ing, whilst the "lock-out" lasts. Be this as
it may, the men in their conduct of the ne-
gotiations with the employers, were in every
way right at the commencement. Nothing
can be worse or more to be deprecated than
the half-brutal off-hand way in which
employers frequently treat working men,
and the joiners acted in a manly and
fitting spirit in resisting this. The mon's
offers to arbitrate were stupidly refused by
the employers, and when accepted, with
.a
condition of being sole appointers of the arbi-
trators, the concession was simply an insult.
Up to the 11th of April, therefore, when aft.
MILTKIN received a letter from Mr. PIPEII
offering fair conditions of arbitration, do
men were in the right and the employers de-
cidedly in the wrong. It must be clear
eto
every sensible working man that arbitration
is, above all other ways, the right way of
settling the disputes of working men and
their employers. A more reference to force by
a strike or a look-out is no security for Jar
tic(); in such a contest the weakest must go

to the wall. Such a settlement almost neces-
sarily includes further fighting, as the con-
quered party is never satisfied with the result.
On the other hand, arbitration is almost sure
to satisfy both sides partially, and leaves
everything open to future friendly adjust-
ment by friendly negociation, whenever new
circumstances warrant the reopening of the
case. There was every reason to believe that
the working men saw this clearly, as at
several trades union congresses the principle
of arbitration has been affirmed by resolu-
tion. In fact, the first offers of the carpenters
and joiners showed that they had faith in
this salutary principle, and desired its adop-
tion.

By what blunder in policy, we ask, was this
disposition departed from? Or why the
mockery of insisting on the two most import-
ant points in dispute being withdrawn from
arbitration? If the men had accepted full
arbitration over their whole case—and any-
thing less is a mere playing with the question
—their arbitrators would have gone armed
with a clear understanding as to the points in
dispute to which they attached the chief im-
portance, and they would have fought for such
a settlement as might be most agreeable and
advantageous to the men. They might not
have secured all they are looking for, but if
their ease had been ably handled—as there can-
aot be much doubt it would have been—they
might have secured, without contest or loss of an
hour or a shilling, the most important portion
of the matter in dispute. As it is, they have
discredited a principle to which working men
should cling with tenacity and in good faith,
and have entered, on a contest whioh, whether
won or lost, must entail on them and their
families serious loss and suffering, to say
nothing of the general disturbance to industry
which strikes and lock-outs invariably bring
with them.

At the present moment the battle is not being
fought by the whole of the forces on either
side, but there is every likelihood, if it goes on,
all will be drawn in, to the injury of all. If it
be not absolutely too late, something ought yet
to be done to rectify the mistake which has been
made. We do not ask the men to stand still one
moment or to sleeken their efforts in the least,
and if Lthe fight must go on, our hearty
sympathy will be with them, and our earnest
desire that they may win will not suffer
diminution. But wo suggest that they ought
to have the courage and magnanimity to
ask for a parley—or rather to appoint
some person lin whose judgment and
honour they can rely—to open nego-
tiations with the employers, not because
they dread the issue of the battle,
but incense, having taken a false step, they
wish to repair it in a manly and considerate
way. Men may go wrong—all men, whether
singly or in association, do; but honest and
wise men, when they discover their error, are
never afraid to make an effort to put them-
selves right. Such an attempt will be sure
to strengthen the hands of the men by winning
for them the goodwill of the public, and it
cannot in any way tell to their disadvantage.
A partial victory by arbitration will be better
than a complete triumph by force. It will
be more secure, and will be a step forward in
the direction of that independence for which
working men have been so long struggling.
We ask the joiners and carpenters in all
sincerity to consider this sugg cation, and we
press it on them the more earnestly, because
It will tend to exalt and make permanent
those mutual discussions and, settlements
between employers and employed, from which
alone we can hope for that thorough identifi-
cation of interests on which our best hopes in
reference to the future industry of the country
rut.

One more suggestion of a minor kind, which
is, that those discussions, such as that which
appeared in the Daily News of last Monday,
should be carried on in private. Their pub-
lication is injurious and discrediting. Such
matters ought to be settled in Committee—
certainly without affording opportunity to
picturesque writers in the Press to make sport
for those disposed to laugh at working men's
follies. Proverbially, it has been settled that
it is alwoysthe best plan to wash dirty linen at
bonie.

DISRAELI AT THE CRYSTAL PALACE.
WE do not observe anything particularly
new or strange in the great Conservative and
Constitutional demonstration of Monday last,
except it be the midsummer madness which
suggested the formation of "ladies' associa-
tions." Somewhere between one and two
hundred men of all ranks mustered at the
Palace Hotel; and over a thousand dined to-
gether in what Mr. RAIRES called "the
largest glass case in:England." The "election
victories of last year" were the inspiration and
the theme. Lord GEORGE HAMILTON ventured
to state that "the Liberal party are very much
dissatisfied with their present leader ;" and,
what was a bolder thing, to prophesy
that a "General Election would result in
the return of the Conservatives to power."
The Earl of DENBIGII, who might be
an authority concerning those who are of
the same Church as himself, explained that
the Roman Catholics had been driven into the
Liberal ranks by mismanagement, but were
gradually coming round to the Conservative
side; and, by way of suggesting what may
come to pass when that coming round shall be
completed, he drew from his more recent
reading of history the conclusion, that "the
great victories of this country had been won
by Catholic monarchs and Catholic states-
men." Unfortunately for this view, the most
recent of the former was that wonderful
conqueror, JAMES the SECOND! However,
according to the noble Chairman, "there is
not a single thing on which the Liberal party
are united, nor a single thing on which the Con-
vative party are not united. The illustration
of this text was left to Mr. DISRAE Lr, who,
to make the picture complete, ought to have
been witnessed in the glass case interlocked with
Mr. CA.VENDESIL BENTINCIC in mutual em-
braces. Instead of this, he could only exhibit
himself on the right hand of the oh air, with
Lord Mayor GrnnoNs on the left.
The able leader of the party addressed
himself to the state and prospects of the
"constitutional cause." Starting from the
deserved overthrow which followed the adop-
tion of principles of exolusionals and restric-
tion, his object was to show that the Liberals
relied for success on the substitution of
cosmopolitan for national principles. Th e
real aim of that party, however, is
to change institutions under the plea
of reform, and to sweep away manners and
customs under the pretence of progress. At
length, the people have found them out, an d
both doubt and hate them. The "Tory party,"
on the other hand, is national, or it is nothing.
—neither noble nor democratic; it is composed
of all classes, is, in fact, Nation al.
What, thou, is the prospect before this
national, this all- chums combination? Three
objects lie before it. To maintain the institu-
tions of the country; to preserve the empire ;
and to raise the condition of the people. In
the first of these were included the throne,
tho legislature, and the church. All these
the Liberals have in turn continually
attacked; all of these, therefore, the Nationals
arc to defend. One representative of the
people has brought this charge upon the
whole Liberal party, so far as the
Monarchy is concerned; while, on the other
hand, the countless millions of Conservative
working men are vouched in proof that the
Nationals will uphold it. The House of
Lords, again, has been assailed in every
manner, as anomalous and as pernicious; but
the people, "in my opinion, " says Mr.
DISRLELI, have discovered that a second
chamber is necessary to Constitutional Go-
vernment, and they accept that which exists
as comprising "all the virtues" and "all the
accomplishments" in a perfection which
no theory could either supply or prepare. "In
my opinion" again, the liberty of England
depends much upon the landed tenure of the
soil by a class which can defy alike despots
and mobs, and must be patriotic from its very
nature and circumstances.
But the exposition which Mr. Disukur gave
of the Representation as one of the institutions
of the country which have everything to dread
from the Liberals and everything to hope
from the Nationals, was, perhaps, the most
interesting portion of his speech. We have had
two Reform Acts. The first was the work of

the Liberals, who, "in my opinion," began
by "abolishing all the franchises of the work-
ing classes." That is to say, the working classes
were disfranchised in Galton and old Sarum.
But were they disfranchised in Manchester,
Leeds, Birmingham, and Sheffield? No; the
only thing that can be truly said is, that, in
the gift of the franchise for the first time to
those and such like places, the working classes
were omitted. Mr. DISRAELI talks of "the
Act of Parliamentary Reform of the year
1887 ; " but in our opinion, the Bill of that
session did not become an Act. However,
Bill or Act, he assures us, that it was founded
upon a confidence that the great body of the
people are Conservative; in answer to which
we can only say, that, if the Nationals
ever show themselves to be truly national,
they will find the nation of their party. In
the meantime, Mr. DISRAELI has the discre-
tion not to claim, except by this bare allusion
to "the act of Parliamentary Reform of the
year 1867," the credit of that second Reform
Act under which we are now living, and on
which Lord GEORGE HAMILTON builds his
confident hopes of the return of the Conserva-
tives to power.
Of all the institutions of the country, the
Church is that which has au& red most at
Liberal hands, and has most to hope from
National nurture. It is conveniently for-
gotten, however, that the decimation of the
Irish Bishops by the late Lord DERBY pre-
ceded the disestablishment of the Irish
Church by the living Mr. GLA.DSTONE. But
that noble Earl has gone to his account,
and Mr. DISRAELI is now not the
second man in the Tory party, but the
first among the Nationals. No society, he
assures us, is safe unless there is a public recog-
nition of the Providential Government of the
World and of the future responsibility of man.
This being so, how does it follow that we must
have an Established Church, especially of the
present or of any other type ? Instead of
answering or anticipating this question, he
applies, himself to show that the clergy,
formerly, as he admits, "asleep," but now
charged with only too much activity, are bend-
ing all their efforts towards making the Church
really that which it has heretofore been in
name only; that is, National. Now, to many
observant oyes, the clergy seem to be pulling
in directions so opposite one to another, that,
instead of a National Church, a number of
fragments appears inevitable. To the eyes of
Mr. DISRAELI, on the contrary, looking,
as perhaps he does, through a pair
of " comprehensive" spectacles with which
Primate TAIT may have accommodated him,
all these contentions and divariations of the
clergy assume the form of one united "effort
of the Church to represent every mood of
the spiritual mind of man." The illness of
the HErn-APPARENT worked the miracle of
uniting Christians, Turks, Hindoos, and
Parsecs, in prayer to GOD for one end. The
clergy, under the philo-Hebraist leadership
of Mr. DisnAnr, are, it seems, about to work
a greater, and to bring in Dr. ADLER and
Duke's-place into the bosom of the Established
Church!

As to the preservation of the Empire, of
course the Liberals have done nothing at all
except to accelerate its disintegration, and we
may console ourselves as well as we can with the
fact, that after forty years' continuous effort in
that direction, so many stones of the structure
still hold together. What, then, are the
Nationals going to do for the elevation of the
people? In order to this, you must reduce
their hours of labour and harmonise their
toil. But the principles of economic truth
must not be violated. Practically, however,
you must begin by rescuing them out of the
hands of the Liberals, who are in a selfish con-
spiracy to work them to death. Yes, these
were "the most blatant and loud-mouthed
leaders of the Liberal party." Now, Mr.
DisnAru, much as he is concerned for Crown
and Church, Lords and Commons, has for his
chief anxiety the health and comfort of the
people. They must be better lodged; they
must have air, light, and water; their labour
must be inspeeted, their food purified, and
their "habits of excess and brutality" checked
and cured. But, as to political rights,
the only question, is whether they have

'

not already too much. Such is the anti-
climax to which Mr. DISRAELI" brought
this second speech. The first, which was in-
ter-sessional, !made all turn upon sanitary
regulations; the second, which is intra-ses-
sional, is but a variation on thelsame theme.
The people, we can answer for them, will
thank anybody who raises their condition,
let him be content to call himself Liberal or
aspire to the title of National ; but their
hopes will not be fed, nor will their hunger
be appeased, by a long procession of artfully
arranged words, which end in nothing better
than the call for "a decision between national
and cosmopolitan principles."

THE IRON TRADE AND ITS PROFITS.
WE give the following paragraph on the
iron trade from the Bradford Observer of the
20thl1n8t.:—

WO LVERILUIPTON, Wednesday.—Bar iron was
this afternoon declared at the extraordinary and
unprecedented height of £l4 12s. 6d., by Bin
Dudley, and £l4 by Messrs. Barrows. Foundry
goods were up 20s. A ninth advance was an-
nounced on galvanized and tin goods, 20 per cent.
on locks, and 16 per cent. on curry combs. Cut
nail? were 20s. dearer, and forged nails and
chains, and every other hardware product, were
higher. Nevertheless, sellers were afraid to book,
and vendors of pigs would only accept handsome
bids, they offered nothing. Miners' wages will be
advanced.

This is worth careful notice, as it gives
some insight into the profits made by
manufacturers of iron, and may lead to some
sort of reflection as to foreign competition and
its effect on our home trade, and especially as
this is effected by the price of labour.
SIDNEY SMITH, a short time since, took the
trouble of pointing out to the irounmsters the
oppressions they were suffering from their
men; and as he is the secretary of an asso-
ciated body of those masters, whose object is
to keep the men in check, it may not be amiss
to ask him for some explanation of the facts
stated in the passage we have quoted.
We do not desire to pry too closely into the
affairs of the employers, but we really should
like to be informed as to the cost price of a
ton of bar iron. We ask this question because
we desire to ascertain, with as much accuracy
as possible, whether the danger through
foreign competition which we so frequently
hear spoken of arises from high wages on the
part of the workers, or high profits extorted
by the makers and merchants from purchasers.
We take it that the price per ton of cost in the
make of bar iron is about the same now that it
has been for the last thirty years. The only
varying quantity as an element of cost is
wages, and as wages in the manufacture of
such an article is but a small proportion of
the whole cost, it would be instructive to
I know how much 10 or even 20 per cent. as
advance in wages would amount to on the
whole cost of production. At any rate, we
know that the average price of bar iron over
the whole of the year 1851, was £5 11 B. 6d.
per ton. If Mr. SIDNEY Smart or the Messrs.
CREED and WILLIAMS see this, we ask them
to make a note of it, and tell us what profits
were realized during this said year on the sale
of bar iron. Possibly, they did not amount
to much, as.the year was a bad one. It may
be that they yielded nothing; though that is
by no means a likely case. Indeed, for many
reasons, it may be regarded as impossible. To
show these champions of masters' rights,
however, that we do not wish to press our
ease unduly, we are willing to throw in is. 6d.
per ton, and count the net cost of production
as £6.

Having done this, we now ask our readers
to go back to the paragraph quoted at the
opening of this article, and note the price of
this same commodity. "Bar iron," writes
the Wolverhampton correspondent of the
Bradford Observer, "was this afternoon de-
clared at the extraordinary and unprecedented
height of £l4 128. ad." Now, one of the
simplest rules of arithmetic will make it plain
to the most stupid that £6 as cost taken
from £l4 128. ad. as selling price, leaves as
balance of profit XS 12s. 6d. per ton. If it
does not leave this, will SIDNEY Slant
or any other clever man inform us why
and wherefore? There may be a screw loose in
our calculation somewhere; if so it can be
pointed out. We do net wish to exaggerate
profits, nor in any way to charge against the
employer what he does not in reality receive.

Were we to turn, round on these who are now
realizing these profits and charge them with
driving the trade out of the country, what
would. they say? They would most likely
inform us that we were idiotic persons, and
that silence would be our best policy. They
might say, and properly so, that the iron is
their commodity, and they have a right to get
as much for it as they can in an °Pen market,
and. if Frenchmen, Belgians, and Prussians
can make it cheaper for themselves,, let them
do so.

We have nothing to urge against this.
There is no satisfactory reply to such a state-
ment of the case, )3ut what we object
to is, that when working men ask for an ad.:
vanced price for their commodity, these very
men, anti their interested friends, turn round
on them, charge them with unreasonableness,
and tell them they are driving our trade into
the hands of foreign rivals. Clearly sauce
for the goose is not sauce for the gander with
these gentlemen, for whilst they cry out with
dismay at an advance of 10 per cent, on wages,
which at most would not be more than 1 per
cent. of the whole cost of the article, they
themselves pocket, no doubt with great satis-
faction at heart and Baena), of countenance,
125 per cent, on the gross cost of production.

Many lessons might be read to trades'
unionists and others from these figures. We
have pointed out what an advance of wages
means; we point out also what an advance in
profits somQtimes amounts to, and, whilst
doing this, we turn to men in the building
trades now on strike and looked out—ere long
to be feeling the painful pressure of a
shortened income—and ask them how and
why it is they have done nothing to organize
their labour ?—how and why it is that their
highest and most successful attempts are for
the organization of idleness ? 'Nine hours in-
stead of ten is a desirable reform ; ninepence
per hour instead of eight is also desirable.
But why stand idle to get this instead of
organizing and going to work—sending ill
tenders and taking contracts, and adding to
their incomes, in the shape of pro4t, what
would bring not comfort only into their
homes, but manly independence into their
lives.

articles.title: MEN OF THE ENFIELD FACTOItY AND THE GOVERNMENT.
articles.text:
THE MEN OF THE ENFIELD FACTOItY
AND THE GOVERNMENT.

THE Government has not yet taken the hint
we threw out the other day, as to the propriety 1
of adopting the nine hours system in the
various public establishments under its control.
It is not desirable that there should be strikes
At Woolwich, at Enfield Factory, but matters
are nevertheless Moving in that direction, and
the moment for a 'collision will sooner or later
arrive, however desirous the men may be to
avoid it, unless those in authority make pro-
vision for meeting their demands.
Wo ask those who have it in their power to
decide the matter to look at the position.
This demand on the part of the men is not self-
originated--it is simply the inevitable desire of
the men to place themselves on a level with their
fellow working men everywhere throughout
the kingdom. Industry is relieving itself of
a portion of the oppressive weight Which it has
hitherto Carried. Such. attempts as have been
made have succeeded, and this sueeess etn-
braces nearly every leading branch of industry
in the kingdom. Is it not evident, therefore,
that what has been gained elsewhere must be
given in the Government works. And. if so,
is it not utterly stupid on the part of the
Government to allow their officialS to keep
haggling, and shifting, and deferring, instead
of frankly complying at once.
If they suppose that working men do not
feel this huxtering as, an insult, they are
greatly mistaken. Or if they think it will not
beget active hostility, they will some day find
out their error to their cost. To enforce worse
terms on their men than exist elsewhere, is in
the end to get rid of the best and keep only
the worst, and this is certainly, so far as the
nation is concerned, not d.esirable. It is also
to lose the goodwill of the workers, and this,
whenever a strain comes, will be a loss the
nation ought not to be made subject to,
through shabby notions of false economy.
Besides, as a simple matter of personal
prudence, there should be no hesitation, An

individual ease may serve to show this. Sir
Hum STORKS had great difficulty to find a seat
whoa his presence in the House of Commons
was felt to be desirable; and. when he suc-
ceeded at Colehester it was considered., by the
friends of the Administration that a great
point was gained. Now, however, Sir HENRY
does not seem disposed to listen to the claims
of the men under his control, or to see to the
settlement of the dispute at present existing
between them and the heads of departments
under him. We do not know the precise
routine established by Red Tape in such oases,
but we are quite sure that if Sir HENRY
exerted the power he actually possesses, a
settlement might soon be made. The time is
not far distant when Sir HENRY STORKS will
have to put himself again before the electors,
and there is nothing more certain that that
what he does now will be remembered
then.

On last Saturday a meeting of the Govern-
ment operatives at Enfield was unanimous
and enthusiastic for the nine hours, but
there was no evidence that the Government
was disposed to comply with the men's re-
quest. A very slight publio
.pressure would
souu decide the matter. A public meeting
or two amongst the large trades union
bodies, or, a memorial from those who
have already secured the nine hours, to the
Government, or, better still perhaps, a depu-
tation waiting on the head of the department
where the power lies to deal with the matter,
would be almost sure to obtain the object in
.view; if the men who formed that deputation
belonged to the leading unions of. the king-
dom. Wherever these have the power to ex-
tend the nine hours they ought to use that
power, as the more complete the extension the
more secure this great gain to working men
Will be made. This gain of time to the
, worker is worth everything else. Once con-
quered, it earl never be yielded. Let it
therefore be secured, by a steady pressure for-
ward so long as a •single inch of ground
remains to be won. kbove all things, let the
men at Woolwich, Earleld, and elsewhere
thoroughly organize their numbers and press
their demands unceasingly, and their victory
must be certain though it may be slightly
delayed.

THE POSTAL AND TELEGRAPH
SERVICE.

SO3IE few months since the men in the !
Telegraph Service resisted. what they believed
to be oppressions in that service. And they
were beaten, "Mr. SCIIDLUORIC employed
rather more than the full power at his dis-
posed, and. in the end succeeded in overcoming
them. Now, the men of the Post-office and Tele-
graph Service are anxious to bring the condi-

general conditions of labour throughout the
country. Their task is so delicate and (Moult
that it is almost impossible. For the most
part they are unskilled men brought early
into the postal service without having learned
any trade, They would, therefore, be almost
helpless if east out by the postal authorities—
and so watchful is the supervision under
which their labour is carried on that any act
looking in the least like an attempt at cora-
bination is punished by immediate dismissal.
It IS true that the authorities are justified in
seeing that the public service is not in-
terfered with. But then if the men are to be
held rigidly to their work Without the privilege
Of uniting for mutual protection, they ought to
be So treated as to render union unnecessary.
We by no means say that the men are right in
submitting to this; on the contrary, we would
counsel a general and firm union amongst the
men, which could defy authority if arbitrarily
or oppressively °itemised. This is by no means
an *possible thing, and we believe the oppor-
tunity is now opened to them to do so, But
whatever may come of this, there is so much
to complain of by way of over work, under pay,
and Sunday work, that the aid of working
men everywhere should be given to the post
office employes for the attainment of their
object. Mr. GLADSTONE and his party may be
sure that unless they act humanely and
thoughtfully in regard to the condition of
Governmclit employes, Mr. Drsus.Bas bid
madb at t e Crystal Palace will be Itooepted.

The day of social polities has come, and iti

be desired by Liberal politicians that the

the work wisely. This subject must not be
allowed to. drop. The condition of the Post-
office and Telegraph people is too large an iteni

MIL IWARTHUIt'S MOTION ON FIJI.
Mn. M'ARTaun, the kind-hearted member
for Lambeth, has made a persevering, but
unsuccessful struggle to bring the Fiji Islandi
under British protection. First, he moved
for a Protectorate pure and simple; then he
introduced the alternative of annexation;
and, thirdly, perceiving no prospect of carry-
ing either, he expressea a wish to withdraw
the matter altogether. The Opposition, how-
ever, refused him leave, and his motion was
negatived by 135 to 81,
Mr. APAnyntra supported his proposal by
a series of interesting facts; principally rely
ing upon the position of the group in the
Pacific Ocean, and in relation to Australia,
San Francisco, and British Columbia. They
form, in fact, the key of Polynesia, and if
placed, like Tahiti, in the hands of a foreign
Power, might do England serious mischief.
At the same time, the mover did net by any
means conceal the fact of the interest that the
Wesleyan Missionary Society has in the
maintenance of British influence, in the
islands. Even on the ground of economy, tO,
take Fiji under protection, would cost lose
than to put down kidnapping, The King;

did the manufacturers and the colonists.
The motion, nevertheless, was opposed by
the UNDETI-SECRETSRY for the Colonies "
backed by the PnrstE MINISTER. The former
denied that the Fijians wished either protec-
tion or annexation; the Xing, who desired '
it, was only one of forty chiefs, the rest of
whom deprecated it. The groupe comprises
some two hundred islets; and all that England
wants there iä a coaling station for steamships.
Ono act of annexation would necessitate
ulterior steps. Now Zealand had cost us
twenty millions; and that was a eaution. The
former refusal of annexation had led to
the formation of a kind of European Govern-
ment with which it would be unadvisable to
interfere. A protectorate had all the faults of
an annexation, without any of its benefits.
If the existing island governMent would help
the British Admiralty in putting down the
"labour traffic " (otherwise slave trade), that
-wail& be the best that would at present be
attempted. . It at 6;otno future time, the
colonists and the natives of Fiji should.unite
in the wish to annex the groupe to Great
Britain, it might be the duty of the Govern-
ment to entertain the question; but the pre-
sent experiment ought to be all Owed fair
play.

- Mr. GLADStONE occupied himself with shelv-
ing the unfairness of throwing upon Govern-
ment the choice between protection and an-
nexation; to both of which, however, they
were opposed, He was surprised at their own
supporters wanting to load them with more
responsibility, when what theylay under was
more than they could already rid themselves
of. The PREMTER made merry with the rather
loose arguing of Mr. KINNAIRD , whom he
asked to produce his eredentialk if he
really was charged with an embassy from
the Prime chief of Fiji. Mr. GL-
STONE principally relied upon the New
Zealand objection. If two islands, divided by
one narrow channel, had cost us so much
treasure and blood as the result of annexation
really asked for by the native authorities,
what temptation was there to undertake, With-
out any such invitation, the government of
two hundred islands separate from each other
and. under the authority and influence -of
nobody knew how many independent chiefs?
In fine, if civilisation has made so much
progress without foreign interference, why not
leave well alone? This was the answer of the
Government; and, unless sorke adverse foreign
Power be about to make mischief, why meddle
at all?

THE BALLOT BILL.

Tun Ballot Bill has passed the House of
Lords and been sent down with amendments
tb the House of Commons, in which those
amendments will .probably be considered on
Monday next. No doubt, from the most
material of these, the representative Chamber
will dissent; and perhaps the Peers will yield.
In this case, the Bill will go for the Royal
assent much as it left the House of Commons;
intl. the next General Election, which is to
bring the Tories into power, if Lord GEORGE
HAMILTON be a prophet, will be elected under
tile Ballot.

THE GENERAL BAPTISTS ON THE
BENNETT JUDGMENT.

TRH General Baptists, in full conference at
Nottingham, have been the first among Non-
conformist bodies to take distinct note of the
BENITZTT judgment. They have no pleasure
In separation for its own sake, they say; but
they dare not suffer themselves to be compre-
hended in a Church which saps the spiritual
life by deriving maintenance from the State.
Bad as the mechaniCal connection between
Church and State is in itself, the recent
deliverance of the highest Judicial Bench in
the realm has made it absolutely unbearable.
That judgment proves that the English Church
is Romanist as well as Eationalistio. Turning
to the great questions agitating human
society, liberty and equality are the two key.
facts of the age. Inquiry, science, the press,
and the platform are declared to be free; trade
is becoming free; and Parliament and the
Church will soon be free. Having adverted
to pauperism as a matter in which we have not
improved one jot upon the days of WlLLuat
the THIRD, the PRESMENT said the most
striking and impressive feature of modern life
was the declared war between the-captains and
the soldiers of industry. Than this struggle
there is nothing more 'momentous on earth;
and the spirit in which it is conducted and the
condition of final adjustment are vital to the
future of England and of the world.

TUE Jesuits, if foreigners, are to be ex-

of the Empire has adopted the law for that
purpose as passed by the Reichstag of Prussia.
The decree will be presently issued. The
measure was first passed by the Federal Connell.

Its acceptance by the former thus strengthened
proves what is the national sentiment. Prince
BifiliißClE is supported by his *hole race. The
Jesuits are named, but the Church is meant.
As the POPE says, "Persecution has begun in
Germany, but the Catholics display courage."
Yes, the Bishop of ERMELAND has temerity
enough to refuse obedience to the orders of
the Minister of Publio Worship, on the ground
that he can obey the law of the land only
when in accordance with the law of GOD.
Who makes the law of the land? Its ap-

It comes, therefore, to this—that the priests of
Rome will not be bound by any ties of allegi-

RISING PROSPECTS OF REPUBLICAN-
ISM IN FRANCE.

M. TEETERS, for the present, remains clearly
steadfast to the Republic of France. The
konarehioal party in the Assembly is numer-
ous; in fact, a majority. But then, if it came
to the selection of a King, they would be
divided among themselves. The Duke de
BROGLIE, himself Orleanist, declares that they
are not now Monarchists, but simply Con.
servatives, presenting an energetic resistance

to the Radical yoke that threatens Fratee.
What nonsense to pretend that this is not to
be Monarchical. However, the Duke and hie
present associates will respect M. TRIERS as the
chosen chief of the State; but, if Conserva-
tive principles be found in danger, they will
then do tbeir duty, and do it to the end. In
the meantime, the Radical Republicans, as
they are called, in contradistinction, of what
is Communistic or Red, in recollection or in
fact, are sending up addresses of congratula-
tion to the PRESIDENT OR the firmness which
he manifests; while those in Versailles are
celebrating the birthday of lidera, the Repub-

articles.title: EIGHT HOURS MOVEMENT IN AMERICA.
articles.text:
EIGHT HOURS MOVEMENT IN
AMERICA.

The working men of New York paraded on
Wednesday to the number of 2,000 to 3,000 in
honour of the Eight aour Movement. They ex-
pected at first to turn out in much larger numbers,
but differences arose between tho trades unions as
to the expediency of parading at all, many oppos-
ing it. The trades that had achieved their victory
did not appear in the line to any extent, the men
preferring- to remain at work; so that the proces-
sion was made up mainly of those who are still on
strike. They marched quietly. through the
principal streets, and were gazed at by large
crowds on the side walks. The piano :manufac-
turers, who are making the mast effectual resist-
ance to the New York eight-hour strike, held a
meeting on Wednesday while the procession was in
line, and declared their...determination to hold out.
The piano-tnakers are nearly all idle, and, unlike
most of the other trades in this strike, it seemed
very much on Thursday as if they would have
to yield to the employer.

articles.title: BUILDING SOCIETIES' BILL.
articles.text:
THE BUILDING SOCIETIES' BILL.

A conference of representatives of building
societies throughout the country was held at
the Westminster Palace Hotel, a few days
ago, with a view to defeating the Government
amendment of the above Bill. Mr. E. T.
Gourley, 31.P.i presided.

There was a large attendance, including
the following members of Parliament :—Messrs.
Eastwiek, Locke, Watney, Sheridan, Rath-
bone, H. Lewis, Stevenson, Beaumont, Wing-
field, Baker, Kay-Shuttleworth, M. T. Bass,
M'Cullagh Terrens, Headlam, Trevelyan,
Arruitstead, Birley,
.and T. Brassy ; Sir Har-
court Johnstone, Sir J. Ogilvey, and Sir D.
&lemons ; Colonel Beresford and Viscount
Bandon.

The 'Chairman said the object of the 1341
was to determine any doubts with reference
to the borrowing powers of building societies,
and that of the meeting to .consider the pro-
posals of the Government, which introduced
an entire change of the mode in which thoie
societies had hitherto been worked. The
most convenient course to pursue he thought,
was to form a committee to decide whether,
under the circumstances, it was advisable to
press forward the Bill through Parliament thie
session, or to delaY further action in the
matter until tho next. His own opinion was
that it was best to press the Bill this session.
He then read a letter *which he had received
from Mr. Winterbotham, M.P., Under-score-
tug for the Home Department, who said that
Mr. Bruce Could not assent to the provieions
of the Bill for the following reasons :—That
the Government declined to undertake the
powers and responsibilities proposed to be
entrusted to the registrar, preferring much a
'system of open registration, with no special
restrictions on the constitution and powers of
societies, and consequently no responsibility
on the part of the Government; that the re-
strictions on borrowing proposed were wholly
illusory; and that no sufficient reason was
apparent for continuing the present_ excep-
tional constitution and privileges of building
societies. Mr. Bruce's opinion was that legis-
lation should be postponed till next year. Mx.
Highom, secretary of the. Building Societies'
Protection Society, moved, and Mr. C. Binyon
seconded, a resolution whieh declined to en-
tertain the suggestions of the Government.
Mr. Strong, of Newcastle, Mr. Watson of the
same town, and others, opposed the resolution
preferring to make terms with the Govern,
ment, but the majority of those present were
in its favour; and a subsequent resolution,
likewise carried, asked the support of members
of Parliament in passing the Bill. •
