THE WEEK'S NEWS.

To the Democratic State Conventions en-
dorsing the nomination of Mr. Horaee Greeley
as President Tnnst now be added those of
Kentucky and Minnesota.

Boston having already heard the bands of
England and Germany at the Jubilee, gave the
next place of honour to France. The 'band
of the Garde Republicaine played in presence
of 40,000 persons, and the choral ends are
described as splendid:

A reception was given by her Majesty to the
Burmese Ambassadors at Windsor the other
day. They partook of luncheon, and, after
the audience, returned to London.

A settlement was arrived at in the great
will case of Thwates v. Tebbitt, which had
occupied the Court of Probate during two
successive days. The counsel for the plaintiff,
who is a clergyman of the Church of England,
announced that in consideration of the great
expense which would be entailed by fighting
out the case, he acted on the suggestion of
Lord Penzance, and compromised it by accept-
ing a verdict for the defendant, Mrs. Tebbitt,
sister of the testatrix, who was accordingly
allowed to take out letters of administration.

After the strong recommendation of the
jury, it will scarcely cause surprise to learn
that the capital sentence on Marguerite
Dixblanc, the Park-lane murderess, will not
be carried out, the Home Secretary having
advised its commutation to that of penal
servitude for life.

• England was successful in the contest for
the International Challenge Trophy, at the
rifle gathering at Edinburgh. The English
team made 1,194 points, the Scotch 1,191,
and the Irish 1,116, firing at ranges of 200,
NO, and 600 yards.

What is, familiarly known as the Edmunds'
Scandal came before the Court of Queen's
Benet, in the form of an action for libel
brought by the plaintiff, who was formerly
reading clerk in the House of Lords, against
Mr. Oladatone, the Chancellor of the Ex-
chequer, and Mr. Stansfeld. The charges
complained of wore contained in a Treasury
minute and certain State papers, and wero to
the effeet that the plaintiff had, during his
thirty-one years' tenure of office, appropriated
,£99,819 Bs. 10d. of public money. The
defendants pleaded not guilty and a justifica-
tioa. Mr. Edmunds conducted his case in
person, and occupied the whole day in reading
a voluminous statement, which was several
times challenged, but at length allowed by
Mr. Justice Mellor to proceed, by way of
letting the plaintiff tell his own story. Not
being able to prove his case sufficiently, Mr.
Edmunds was non-suited,

Certain French peasants, accused of having
furnished intelligence to the Germans during
the late war, and betrayed to thorn seine
National Guards, who were in •consequence
shot, have been tried by court-martial, and
senteneed, one to death, and two others to ten
and five years' penal servitude. One was
acquitted.

Autumn mane:mitres are, it is said, to be
held in Austria on a grand scale this year.
The whole Bohemian army is to participate,
and the special objeet proposed is testing the
new organization for provisioning the army
and the field telegraph. system.

Austria and Russia have each had a hearing
at the Boston Festival, and in either case the
result has been most successful. At the
Austrian concert on Friday Madame Eudora-
dorfr sang; the British band played, and the
chorus consisted of 16,000 voices, with the
accompaniment of cannon.

Though all the clauses of the Army Bill
have now been passed by the National. As-
sembly at Versailles, the formal third reading
is postponed to await details of the internal
organization of the army. The religious
question was satisfactorily tided over on Satur-
day, when Mgr. DupardouP carried an amend.
raent providing that Government shall secure,
by proper regulations, the free exercise of
religious duties by soldiers and sailors.
Count Itampont, while supporting the prelate's
amendment, protested equally against the
Right assuming a monopoly of religion, and
against the interruptions of the Left during
the speech of Mgr. Dupanloup.

Another journalistic duel has occurred in
Franco. The principals were the editors of
the Republique _Francais and the Eclair. The
former was slightly wounded in the arm.

Certain prominent Republicans, opposed
both to Grant and Greeley, held a meeting in
New York, with only moderate success. A
en3all party nominated Senator Groesbeck as a
candidate. Severaldelegatesolissationed with
the Cincinnati Comer:thou, took part, in tbe
proceedings.

Sir John Pakington presided at the annual
Midsummer Examination of the pupils of the
Commercial Travellers' School, at Pinner, on
which Occasion a portrait of the treasurer, Mr.
Steckdale, w as presented to the institution in
recognition of his great services to the school.

The Rev. J. Purohas, of Brighton, having
entirely ignored the monition which was served
in February last prohibiting him from offici-
ating, in St. j'arnes s Chapel, Brighton, was
further proceeded against by the Church Asso-
ciation before the Judicial Committee of the
Privy Council for the purpose of depriving him
of his benefice. Mr. Purohas did not appear
eithP.r in person or by counsel; and, before
deciding on the ,extreme sentence of depriva-
tion, the committee ordered the ease to stand
over for Dr. Tristram to look into it, no day
being named for its further hearing.

Lord Milton, who is only 33 years of age,
has resigned his seat for the southern division
of the West Riding on account of ill-health.

The
in
in Bedfordshire on Tuesday re-
sulted m the return of Mr. Bassett, the Liberal
candidate, who took the lead from the begin-
ning. At the close of the poll the numbers
were—Bassett, 2,446; Stuart, 2,248; thus
giving the former a majority of 108.

Mr. S. Cave, M.P., on Tuesday, presented
the prizes to the successful students at Uni-
versity College. According to the report,
there were sir ladies attending the ()lasses,
and there had been a grand total of over
1,100 persons instructed within the course of a
single session.

The University Cricket Match was resumed
on Tuesday, and when Oxford had concluded
their second innings for 150 runs, Cambridge
had won by one innings and 166 runs.

According to the weekly return of the
Registrar-General, the warm weather which
i set non Thursday, the 13th inst. reached its
maximum on Monday, the 17th, and a
decreasing daily excess of temperature was
shown on each succeeding day till Saturday,
when the mean was a trifle below the average.
The mean temperature on Monday was 71.8 deg.,
and 12.8 deg. above the average; the highest
reading of the thermometer in the shade was
86.0 deg., and in the sun 150 deg. Very
little rain was measured in London hut heavy
thunder rain, fell on Tuesday in the Midland
and Northern Counties.

From April Ist to the 22 ud inst. the
Treasury receipts amounted to £17,359,492,
as compared with £15,811,642 in the ' corre-
sponding period of last year. The expenditure
has been £15,308,632. On Saturday last
the balance in the Bank of England. was
£8,907,269.

During the week ending on Saturday last
the mortality in London and twenty other
large towns tn the United Kingdom was at the-
rate .of 22 deaths annually to every 1,000
persons estimated to be living. In the metro-
polis 1,997 births and 1,230 deaths were
registered, the former having been 198, and
the latter 140, below the average. Twenty-
six persons died from small-pox, 41 from
measles,9 foin scarlet fever, 6 from diphtheria,
53 from whooping-cough, 23 from different
forms of fever (of which 2 were certified as
typhus, 11 as :enteric or typhoid, and 10 as
simple continued fever), and 25 from diarrhcea.
Diseases of the respiratory organs caused 352
[ deaths, and 59 personal died from different
forms of violence, no less than nine deaths
having been caused by horses or vehicles in
the streets.

At the Marlborough•street Police-court on
Tuesday, the charge of misconduct brought
against a porter at the Richmond Club by
Major Charteris, a sou of Lord Elcho, was
sent for trial at the Central Criminal Court.
Bail was accepted.

At a banquet in 'Versailles to celebrate the
memory of General floche, IL, Clarabetta made
a epeech, in which be dwelt upon the necessity
of restoring the moral greatness of France,
and of maintaining a strong army and rigid
disoiEline.

It is stated by the Tunes of India that
although the heat in Bombay has not this
year been excessive, it has been terrible in the
North-West Provinces. Cases of sunstroke
have been very frequent; no European can
venture out of doors after nine in the morn-
ing ; and indoors life is almost insupportable.
Birds and. small animals take refuge from the
heat inside the houses, and "crows have
actually been known to drop off the trees from
sheer exhaustion." It is satisfactory to learn
that, notwithstanding the great heat, cholera
has been neither so wide-spread nor so fatal
as in previous years. Small-pox has, however,
committed great ravages, and dengue fever,
which the Times (If India describes as a most
excruciatingly painful disease, has been
prevalent throughout India and British
Burinah.

On Tuesday the Archbishop of Canterbury
presided over a conference of the National
Club to consider the best means of organizing
a general movement in the direction of Sunday
closing. A committee was appointed, on the
motion of Mr. Kennavvay, M.P., seconded by
Mr. Morley, M.P., for the purpose of con-
sidering how best to extend the voluntary
efforts now being made to induce tradesmen,
costermongers, and others to avail themselves
of the Sunday rest.

Mr. Closohen is now on a visit to Liverpool,
where he is the guest of Mr. Rathbone,
M.P. On Tuesday afternoon the right hon.
gentleman was officially received on board the
Minotaur, the flag-ship of the Channel Fleet,
now lying in the Mersey.

Another Liberal candidate—Mr. Farley
Leith—appeared at Aberdeen on Tuesday;
but late in the afternoon, rather than provoke
a division in the ranks of the party, he with-
drew from the present contest.

The London Society of Compositors being
desirous of erecting a club-house for the use of
its members combining all the features of a
literary inaitution, have appealed to .the
members of both Houses of Parliament, and
to other influential persons, for assistance in
carrying out that object, and in response to
that appeal have received the liberal donation
of £25 from Mr. J. Walter, M.P.

OA Saturday evening, about half past nine,
a young man named. Alfred Hibbs, was
drowned in the Thames. Ho and a friend
named Turnbull had taken a boat from Putney
and rowed towards Hammersmith Bridge.
After rowing some 4me, they resolved to
bathe. In a few minutes Turnbull noticed
that the deceased bad got beyond his depth
and was sinking. Ile stood panic-stricken for
a few moments, and then ran to the shore to
push out the boat, but ho was too late. Hibbs
had sunk for the last time, Search was made
for some time for the body, but in vain.
Turnbull, it appeared subsequently, did not
know the address of the unfortunate young
man, nor was any clue afforded by searching
his clothes.

• By command of the Queen, a levee was held
on Saturday at St. James's Palace by the
Prince of Wales, which was very numerously
attended. Presentations thereto are, as usual,
to be considered as equivalent to presentations
to her Majesty. •

The Lord Chancellor's Rectory of Holtnp-
ton-in-Holdernesse, . Yorkshire, has become
vacant by the death of the Rev. John Watson,
M.A. It is worth about 200 a year. The
Vicarage of Welwich, also in the Lord
Chancellor's gift, has become vacant by Mr.
Watson's death. It is worth about £l6O a
year.

• The Glatton turret ship wont out of harbour
on Wednesday, and anchored at Spithead, and
will proceed, the first fine day, to Portland for
the purpose of being subjected to an attack of
the Hotspur upon her turrets. Three shots
are to be tired by the last-named ship, two of
them at the turret of the Olatton, and the
third at the glacis plate, in order the more
completely to test the strength .of the structure
and the effect to be produced by a shot striking
the plate near the base of the turret.

Mr. Paver, inspector, of nuisances, . Guis-
borough, attended on Tuesday before the county
magistrates to receive instructions as to the
disposal of the sixty-three sacks of "Jonathan"
retained in his possession under the conviction
of Jackson and millers, on the 18th
instant. Addressing the Nuisance Inspector,
Admiral Chaloner said :—" Respecting Jona-
than,' or whatever it is, you must burn the
article and return the sacks in which it is con-
tained to the accused. The costs, I see are
very, heavy, being £lB 58., and the fine—X2
—make a total sum of .220 55." Besides the
penalty and costs' the value of the article to
be destroyed is 4.!15 155., making a total
of £3O.

A correspondent at Moscow sends an account
of the visit paid by the Czar. to the Exhibition
in that city. His Majesty arrived on the
night of the 18th, and, was most enthusiasti•
cally received by the inhabitants, the city
being illuminated. The next morning be
attended 'service in the cathedral within the
Kremlin, held a. review of the Grenadier
Guards, and afterwards visited. the Exhibition.
At night the Emperor attended a ball given
in honour of his arrival by 'the Governor-
General. Crowds of persons assembled to see
him pass through the streets, which were
again illuminated.

Colonel Sykes's death was, though rather
sudden, not unexpected by hint. lie was in
the House of Commons but three days before
'he -died, and on going out he. Mt so much
difficulty in walking that he said to Mr.
Whitbread, "Let me lean on you; I am going
home to die."

Jun 28, 1872:

tuallers belonging to the midland counties was
hbld on Friday in Birmingham. The object
of the meeting was to consider the course of
action to be taken now that the Government
Licensing Bill had entered the louse of
Commons. It was generally contended that
the Bill was unsatisfactory in three of its
main features—first, as to the time of dosing,

thirdly,- in reference to the exemption of
grocers from appearance before the magis-
trates on applying for a licence. It was
unanimously resolved that a circular should
be issued to all branches of the United Towns
Association and Licensed Victuallers' Defence
League, asking that influence should bo
brought to bear on members of Parliament'
for the purpose of securing the amendment of
the obnoxious clauses of the Bill.

On Friday the ex-Emperor of the French,'
the Empress, and the Prince Imperial, with
their suite, honoured the annual flower show
at Blackheath with their presence. Their
majesties were received by. Dr. Carr, the
president; John Penn, Esq., in whoie grounds
the show took place; the Rev. Charles
Lawrence, the rector, and other members of
the committee. After inspecting the flowers
and fruit, their majesties visited the Cedars,
the residence of Mr. Penn, where they partook
of some slight refreshment. On leaving, the
daughter of the president, Miss Carr, presented
the Empress with a lovely bouquet. Their
majesties were warmly received, and left
behind them the most pleasing impressions. •

An extraordinary scene occurred at the
Petty Sessions Court,' Tralee, on the occasion
of the trial of two privates of the Kerry
Militia on the charge of forming part of
a riotous assembly who burned the effigy of
Judge Keogh, and committed. a savage assault
on ffead-constable Walker. The building
was thronged by a furious mob, the witnesses
for the prosecution werehooted and threatened,
and the disorder at length reached such a
pitch, that the magistrates had to send for au
armed force of police and clear the court. Th,4
prisoners were committed for trial.

It has been proposed to plane a painted
window in Westminster Abbey to the memory
of the officers and men who went down in the
Captain.

Lord Lyons, the English Arabassaidor- at
Paris, M. de Olozaga, the Spanish Ambassador,
several other political and military dignitaries,
and a large assemblage of distinguished
persons, were present on Tuesday at the
funeral of the Marquise de P-enegua, mother
of the Duchess of Malakoff, who was killed in
the recent accident on the Orleans Railway..

The honour of knighthood has been Om,
ferred'on Mr. James itamsden, of lia.rrow-in-
Farness.

The New Testament Company of Revisers
assembled on Tuesday, in the Jerusatem
Chamber, for their twenty-first session. The
Bishop of Gloucester and Bristol presided.
The Campany proceeded to the revision of the
twenty-second chapter of the Gospel of St.
Luke. The first and provisional revision of
the third Gospel will prof:4l)ly be completed
during the present session.

On Monday next the remainder of the me-
tropolis roads north of .the Thames will b 3
disturnpiked." The Kensington, Hampstead-
road, Islington, and other , gates in the, same
trust were removed on the Ist of July, 1864.
The removals next 'Monday, just eight yeaFs
after, will " disturnpike " the roads between
the metropolis and Cranford Bridge' Ux-
bridge, Bushey, Harrow, Enfield, and Wood-
ford, and sweep away the gates at Chiswick,
Harrow-road, Stamford-hill, Manor House,
and Lea-bridge. -

Lady Mayo has addressed a touching lu‘ter
to the teachers and scholars of the Foluale
Bethune Scheel, Calcutta. The teachers and
girls had addressed her ladyship, who while in
India took a deep interest in the school.

Professor H. S. Oakeley is said to be going
on as well as can be expected, under the care
of Dr. Metcalfe, of Geneva. His injuries are
very severe, the right hip bone being fractured
as well as the kneecap. His brother, Sir
Charles Oaketcy, and Lady Oakeley are witti
him at the St. Nicholas Hotel, liaving started
trom England immediately on receiving the
news of the accident..

- Viscount Royston was thrown out of
carriage on Sunday, evening, and sustained a
severe contusion of his right shoulder and
arm. Ile is progressing favourably.

Tn Germany, ati in England, the strike
movement is ou the iucreuse. A meting of
the Association for the Protection of Mining
Interests was held on •Weduesday with el°B‘3a
doors. The men tit two more mines 'lava

The Bishop of Norwich held his special
visitation on Tuesday in Norwich Cathedral.
In his charge the right rev, prelate strongly
urged upon the clergy the necessity of !doing
all in their power to promote .the religious
education of the people. They must devote
more attention than ever to Sunday-schools in
localities iu which School Boards were formed,
He thought the question of the burial of Dis-
senters in churchyards might be settled satis-
factorily, if it wore approached without party
bitterness upon either side. Upon the subject
of disestablishment, he appealed to both clergy
and laity to rally in support of the Church,
I:nit, he expressed his opinion that Church
reform must also accompany Church defence.
He advocated an extension of the Episcopate'
by the creation of eight new bishoprics, a
reform of Convocation, an,d an augmentation
of small benefices. • "

The members of the Serpentine Swimming
Club decided their annual championship race
in the lake at Ilyda Park on Wednesday
morning. J. B. Johnson, of Leeds, won,
beating D. Ainsworth, Peter Johnson, and
W. Chaphan, who finishei in the order given.
The course was from the grating to the bridge.
and Johnson's time was a trifle under seven-
teen minutes.

The Master and Fellows of Trinity College,
Cambridge, have presented the Rev. Edmund
T. Carey, M.A., curate of Kensington, to the
vicarage of Wymondley-cum-St. Ippolyt's
Hertfordshire. The Bishop of Peterborough
has instituted the Rev. F. B. Newman, M.A.,
late curate of Winston, to the vicarage of
Burton Latimer, near Kettering, in the room
of the Rev. T. Bartlett, M.A.

Mr. John Farley Leith, on Tuesday morning
decided not to divide the Liberal party in
Aberdeen, and therefore withdrew his candi-
dature. The evening meeting, however, com-
posed of working men, was so decidedly in
Mr. Leith's favour, by a vote recording their
conlidenoe in him, and by drawinr, him in an
open conveyance through the town to his
hotel, that he at length placed the matter in
the hands of the electors, stating from the
balcony of the hotel that, if elected, he would
act as their representative.

After the verification of the elections, the
Greek Chamber was "constituted" on Wei-
nes.day. The Minist7 have t majority. M.
Spiro Mille was elected President.

The Courrier de 11 Orient states -that the
Turkish Government has urgedAigr. Kupelia
to obtain absolution- from tho Pope if ho wishes
to remain Armenian Patriarch.

Advices from Cuba state that Colonel ltyan's
expedition in the steamer Fannie has Abated
a landing in Cuba at Nuovitas.

The Burmese Envoy went, on Wednesday,
abcompanied by the Lord Mayor' to the Guild-
hall, Christ's Hospital, and St. Paul's Cathe-
dral, and afterwards lunched at the Mansion
House.

A marriage is arranged between, Lady Ida
Fielding, daughter of the late Earl of Denbigh,
and Malcolm, eldest son of General Sir John
Low, of Clatto Park, St. Andrews.

The first volume of remarkable documents
collected by the Grand Duke Ctesarewieh to
perpetuate the memory of the Russian defence
in the Crimea has just appeared under the
title, "Manuscripts Relative to the Defence of
Sebastapol."

According to a Madrid paper, the first decree
of the Minister for the Colonies, which is about
to appear, will be of a character to recommend
itself to the sympathies of all, being a set of
regulations for carrying out the law for the
abolition of slavery.

On 'Wednesday the Pope received several
foreign Ministers, and subsequently all the
foreign deputations. • His Holiness begged
them to pray for Constantinople, where, he
said, a lamentible schism met with protection
and support. The Pope then gave hip blessing,
particularly mentioning Spain, France, Eng-
land, Italy, and Belgium. The last be called
an exceptional country.

The Spew,. Gazette says that aa early as in
1870 the Pope signed a bull whereby, dispen-
sing with all the customary imperative for-
malities, the Cardinals present in Rome at the
time of his death are commanded to.elect his
successor before his interment.

A romantic marriage took place on Monday
at the Madeleine. During the Commune,
Viscount de Beffry was sent to the lock-up for
refusing to join the insurrectionists. Mdlle,
Guillot, who was acquainted with the
Viscount's mother, determined to rescue him,
and went to the lock-up. She was granted an.
Interview, and so disguised him in a work-
man's suit, which she :had coneealed about
her, that he passed out unnoticed while Mdlle.
Guillot was talking with the sentinel about a
cont ini ere' s place,

Mr. Bennett, of the New York. Herald,
was greatly enriched, as well by the enormous
increase of value in real estate as well as by
the profits of the
.journal: His country seat
at Washington Heights was purchased by
him for about ten thousand pounds, and is,
probably, now -worth one hundred aid fifty
thousand pounds. His whole estate will
probably fall little short of one million of
pounds.

New Zealand, like Ireland, claims to he free
from all venomous reptiles, &a., but a Nelson
journal records the death of an infant from
the prestuped, bite of a spider.

The Tipperary militia have been disgraced
more than once during the past week. A
Captain Quin has eloped with the wife of a
brother officer, and an untrue story of a pursuit
and deadly vengeance prevailed for some dap.
Then some of the soldiers have joined with
the lowest rabble of Cashel in the popular
amusement uf burning Mr. Justice Keogh in
effigy; and a dangerous affray with the con-
stabulary ensued. Summary orders have been
given for the removal of this regiment—
excepting some fifteen or twenty, who are
under lock and key—to the Currngh Camp,
where better behaviour may be hoped for.

Mrs. Stanley Mott, sister of Sir Norman
lfacdonald Lockhart, died in P4ris on
Friday, through the shock she received in the
railway accident at Juvisy. She was travel-
ling with her husband and family from Pau.

The death is recorded of Captain Maynard,
R.N., who has been officially associated with
the International Exhibitions of late years, and
who had charge of a department at Kensington.

Mgr. de Marguerye, Bishop of Autun, has
resigned his charge in consequence of advanc-
ing age, and is about to form part of the
Chapter of St. Denis as Canon, He has occu-
pied the see since 1831.

Her Majesty visted the Hants and Berks
Agricultural Show, in Windsor Home Park,
on Wednesday, and Prince Arthur distributed
the gold medals to the successful exhibitors at
Aston Park, Birmingham.

The Paris papers state that, last Wednesday,
Baron Rothschild received thirty-one waggon-
loads of gold from Germany. We are told
that the banker insisted on having the money
due to him from
,Prussia paid in Specie, in re-
venge for the damage. done by the invaders to
his chateau at Ferrikea.

The Census of the population is terminated
in Paris. A diminution is shown of about
5,600 inhabitants—an insignificant number in
comparison to the total of 1,800,000.

Mr. Wm. Johnston, M.P. for Belfast, sailed
from Londonderry on Friday for Canada. The
Apprentice Boys got up a demonstration in his
honour, which passed off quietly..

The inhabitants of Lisburn of all sects have
sent an address to Sir Richard Wallace, the
beneficent owner of large estates in the
neighbourhood, to represent the borough at
the next vacancy. -Sir Richard, has consented
to do so.

The death is reported of the Rev. P. Con-
way, parish priest of Head fort, county Galway,
one of the clergymen reported in the schedules
appended to the judgment in the matter of the
Galway election petition.

The Times speoial correspondent telegraphs
that "it is said' that the majority of the French
Assembly has resolved to vote in favour of the
tax on raw materials only in the case of its
being absolutely necessary to do so." More-
over, it is asserted that several Deputies of the
Right have resolved to resign their seats, "in
order to make elections necessary in all parts
Of France, with a view to demonstrate exactly,
what are the present opinions of the electoral
bodies."

Synod it was decided that the Presbyterian
Synodal system is the system of the Vrencli

The question of eleetoral quilitications was

British subject recently abducted from Canada
be returned, and indemnified for his false
arrest.

Scandinavian. General Doyle officiates as
acting adnainistrator pending the arrival of
Lord.l)ufferin.

An English steamer, the Gibraltar, from
Cadiz to London, has been lost in crossing the
bar near the Tower of St. Julien, though
happily without fatal result. There were no
passengers; and the crew was saved, but a
valuable cargo lost.

After performing separately on different
evenings, the Biitish, French, and German
Bands played together at the Boston Jubilee,
in conjunction with the American Marine
Band. President Grant was present; and the
audience was in proportion to the gigantic
nature of the entertainment. Seventy thou.
sand seated, and twenty thousand standing,
formed the sum-total of, this truly colossal
audience.

Mr. Du Val, a well-known artist, of Man-
chester, • died suddenly of heart disease on
Saturday week. Among his painting, s are
"Luther burning the Pope's Bull," and "Co-
lumbus in Chains." He was 64 years old.

Two men who lobbed a Persian gentleman
of his watch in Gerrard-street were taken by
the police, and one of thorn let go again. The
magistrate at Marlborough-street, before
whom the case came, commented severely
on this capricious behaviour of the pollee as
likely to lead to a Miscarriage of justice. lie
was informed, by way of explanation, that the
man was known, and would bo found when
" wanted." The case was accordingly re-
manded, though it is scarcely necessary to
say the man did not appear. The less-favoured
of the two was sent to take his trial for high-
way robbery.

Considering the vast and increasing literary
intercourse between Germany and England,
some modification of the present antiquated
and cumbersome laws of international copy-
right is inevitable; and negotiations for a
litorary convention have resulted in the draft
of a treaty being framed by England, which
has been presented to the various Governments
of the Empire for their consideration.

A food strike, which has been going on for
some time in the North of England, begins to
assume serious 'dimensions, and threatens a
violation of the peace. At Consett, which is
one of the head-quarters of the movement,
groups of women severely handled one of their
own sex who ventured to make a purchase
from an obnoxious butcher. The police had
to interfere • but so determined is the resist-
Ance :to high prices that the butchers have
ceased to kill meat, and the population is re-
duced, in spite of itself, almost to a vegetarian
diet.

The death ia announced, at the age of forty-
seven, of Mr. Henry Milbank, son-in-law of
the Duke of Leeds, and grandson of the first
Duke of Cleveland. He was son of Mr. Mark
Milbank, M.P. for Camelford, before the first
Reform Bill.

Mr. Charles Dacres • Bevan, Judge of the
County Court, Cornwall, died at Poway on
Monday, aged sixty-seven. He was called to
the Bar in 1830, was formerly on the Western,
Circuit, Revising Barrister for East Cornwall,
subsequently Recorder of Dartmouth, then of
Falmouth, Holston, and Penzance.

Six magnitieent zebras' valued at £l2O a-
piece, have just arrived at the Jardin d'Accli-
matation. They are a present from the Emperor
of Abyssinia—the stmessor of Theedoros.

In presiding at a meeting of the Diamond
Fields Mission, Bishop Wilberforce of Win-
chester, true to his name' dwelt on thn work
as but tho paying off a long-duo debt, the
cutting-off an entail of curses on our own land
for having maintained and kept alive .the
trade of dealing in men and women.

A coffee-house keeper in Bishopsgate-street,
who exhibited in his window certain exciting
pamphlets and placards directed against the
Catholics and Mr. Gladstone, had his window
broken by an itnpuhive sympathiser either
with the Pope or the Premier. Seine discus-
sion took place when the case came before
Sir It. W. Carden at the Guildhall as to
whether the complainant had a right to ex-
hibit such things. About the folly of doing
so the Magistrate said there could be no
doubt. The aggressor was, however, sen-
tenced to two months' imprisonment with hard
labour.

Signs of a favourableissue to the negotiations
with Germany are afforded by the fact of de-
legates from the financial houses who form the
syndicate for the new loan having had an in-
terview with Mi. Thiers.

Marshal Foray died in .Paris last week. He
was horn in 1804, and entered the school of
Saint Cyr in 1822, Ile was made a general in
1848, and' took part in the coup d'etat of 1851.
Th, deceased was also in command for a short
time before Sebastopol, For the part he played
in the Mexican campaign Ile was made a
Marshal of France. lie had previously been
rn„de a Senator. Of late years his name had
been forgotten.

, FRIDAY.
The Dublin Evening Mail denies the truth
of the reports that Mr. Justice Keogh is about
to retire from the Bench, and that he will not
go on circuit at the approaching Assizes. -
Prince Gortschakoff, who arrived on the
22nd at Berlin, left that city again on Wednes-
day for Interlaken, in Switzerland, where he
will pass the summer.
The Liberals`of South-West Yorkshire have
not yet been able to decide upon a candidate.
The rumour that Mr. Isaac Holden or Mr.
Gaskell would come forward is unauthorised.
Great exertions are being made on behalf of
Mr. Stanhope, the Conservative candidate.
The Rev, J. C. Swayne, MA., late Fellow
of Corpus Christi College, Oxford, write as
follows to a Bristol paper :—" A church cannot
really be Protestant which retains the shadow
of a sacrificing priesthood. I have resigned
holy orders, having long resolved to do so if
the Bennett ease was decided in favour of the
defendant."
The Rev. Mr. Moffat, the African mis-
sionary, was present at a meeting in Sheffield
yesterday, and, speaking of his son-in-law,
Dr, Livingstone, said he felt confident that
distinguished traveller would soon return to
this country to enrich our knowledge of
Central Africa by the fruits of his prolonged
researches.

The Woman's Pence Congruts, called by
Miss Julia Ward Howe, of Boston, U.S.A.,
will hold its opening meeting at Sr. Georgo's
Hall, Regent-street, on Monday, July Bth, at
8 o'clock p.m.

A Renter's telegram from New York says
the impression has revived in the press that
the Treaty of Washington is saved.
At the Salford Borough Court, Mr. Robert
Dodd and Mr. Robert Simons were summoned
for refusing to pay school rates. Both the
defendants pleaded condoientious objections
to paying on the ground that the schools were
denominational. Dr. Roy!, the presiding
magistrate, said the Bench had no discretion,
and ordered that the rate should be enforeed
in both oases.
Resolutions have been passed by the Ballot
Society thanking Mr. Gladstone and Mr.
Forster for their efforts to maintain the
principle of compulsory secret voting, depre-
cating the course which had been taken by
the House of Lords, and expressing a hope
that the Government will drop the Ballot
Bill rather than accede to the amendments of
the Peers.

Viscount Halifax was absent limn Wednes-
day's Cabinet Council.

A meeting of the Governors of Wellington
College was held on. Wednesday in the Palace
of Westminster.

The Conservative candidates for Rochester,
Mr. C. J. Fox and Major Bell, met the electors
on Wednesday night in public meeting, and
had a most flattering reception.
Messrs. Dent, Allcroft, and Co., of Worces-
ter, have intimated to their employes in the
French and English cutting departments, in
Worcester their intention to raise the prices
at the rate of 16 per cent, for all kinds of
cutting. The increased scale of pay will come
into operation next week.

Thirteen &me of strawberries have been sent
from Cornwall during the last four days for tho
London market.

The British ship Dhollerah has been burnt
at sea. The crew were saved.

The total number of messages forwarded
from postal telegraph stations lit the United
Kingdom last week was 304,289, being an
increase of 79,439 over last year.
Professor Beesly states that there are still
in Loudon many French refugees—journalists,
teachers, bookkeepers, &c.—who, having no
handicraft, and being nearly or entirely
ignorant of English, have no means of
supporting themselves.

A house in Chillington-street, Wolver-
hampton, was struck by lightning on
Wednesday afternoon. The chimney was split
asunder, the tire-grate smashed, and the floor
torn up. Four persons were in the room at
tea, but they escaped.
The Pope has addressed a letter to Cardinal
Anton°lli, dated 16th inst., protesting against
the declaration made by the Italian Ministry
of its intention to expropriate the convents.
Another despateh tells us the Pope says the
suppression of religious bodies will be "a
violation of the international law of the
Catholic world." The Pope eoncludes by
requesting Cardinal Antonelli to acquaint the
foreign representatives of, the Vatican with
the state of things, and to protest against acts
menacing the Papacy and Catholicity,

Seven thousand Indians have "taken the
war-path" in Texas.

• In- the neighbourhood• of• Finchley labour
for the purpose of haymaking is so scarce that
the Highway Board for the parish has given
direetions that us many of the men employed
on the roads as can be spared be allowed to
leave nail the haymaking- season is over.

THE POLITICS OF MR, DISRAELI; OR,
THE CHURCH AND THE PEOPLE.
To the Editor of the BF4E-HIVE.

Bra,—lf it is true (and Mr. Disraeli wishes
the people to believe it to be true, on the
authority of some of the most intelligent of
the labouring multitude of England), that
"the policy that would improve the condition
of the people, is more appreciated by the
people than the ineffable mysteries and all the
pains and penalties of the Ballot Bill," then
it must also surely he held to be true by the
most intelligent of the labouring multitude of
England, that the policy that would improve
the condition of the people is more appreciated
by the people than the ineffable mysteries of
Church creeds and dogmas, and all the pains
and penalties of the Act of Uniformity to
establish them,

And if this is allowed to be irresistibly
true, then the people will not surely give their
support to any Church or party who would
impose upon them (reeds and dogmas, which
were ineffable mysteries, as absolutely neces-
sary io be believed (under, the pains and
penalties of an Act of Parliament), prior to or
ea a sine qua non 40, any improvement being
made either in the condition or in the educa-
tion of the people.
And, therefore, the party that would receive
the people's support must neither defend nor
maintain a Church that imposes creeds and
dogmas, that arc ineffable mysteries, upon
the people, but must either be pledged to
reform the Church, or to disestablish it as a
false Church for refusing to put away creeds
and dogmas which are ineffable mysteries,
because such doctrines are wholly needless
and utterly Useless for improving either the
condition or education of the people ;' Silloo
it is a fact and true that what cannot be con-
ceived cannot be received and believed. And
therefore it is a burden intolerable to bear
that creeds and dogmas which are ineffable
mysteries, should be imposed on the people
in the names of religion by authority of the
State, as necessary to be believed under pains
and penalties prior to, or as a sine qua non to,
any improvement being made either in the
condition or in the education of the people by
the rulers of the Church.
Petersham, S.W.

T. G. HEADLEy.

THE LONDON SCHOOL BOARD.

The Board held its ordinary weekly meeting
on Wednesday, in the Council Chamber,
Guildhall; Lord Lawrence presiding.
Mr. Freeman brought up a report frum the
Finance Committee, and, in accordance with
their recoMmendation, moved that Mr. N. H.
Nixon be appointed clerk to the School
Management Committee, at an increased salary
of £2O a year from Lady Day last; that Mr.
Whiddington be appointed clerk to the
Industrial Schools and Bye Laws Committee,
with an increase to his salary of £2O; and
that an additional clerk be appointed for the
general work of the office, at a salary of £BO a
year.
Some objections were made to the proposed
increase of salaries, unless for increased
duties or long service, and it was urged that
the proper course was to revise the salaries
annually. Ultimately the motion was agreed
to, It was further agreed that the Board
should adjourn from the 7th of August to the
28th, and then to the 18th September.
Mr. Freeman then brought up the report of
the Committee on Charitable and other En-
dowments, and moved—

That a copy of the report be forwarded to the
Education Department, accompanied by a letter
stating-that the Board considers that on the whole
the scheme of the Endowed Schools Commissioners
respecting Emmanuel Hospital and the charities
to be united therewith has been drawn in a liberal
spirit, and that it deals fairly with the various
charities proposed to be amalgamated; also to
suggest that alterations should be made as fol.
low :—Tho establishment of a higher form—equi-
valent to a sixth or seventh—for a lithited number
of
.promising pupils, enabling them to reach the
university; an increase of the standard of the
entrance examination; a considerable extension of
the school age (which the Commissioners have
fixed at 14) ; an alteration in the composition of
the governing body, so as to incorporate with the
present managers persona from outside. That
copies of the report, and of the letter sent to the
Education Department with reference to the
scheme respecting Emmanuel Hospital and the
charities proposed to be united therewith, be for-
warded to the Endowed Schools Commissioners.
Mr. S. Geyer thought they ought to
have the scheme of the Corporation of
London .(the guardians of the Charity from
the time of Queen Elizabeth) side by side with
that of the Commissioners, which had been
condemned by the House of Lords, because
it substituted the test of examination for
that of poverty—thus presupposing means to
educate. But he contended that the Boerd
had, nothing to do with the matter, which
belonged to an authority entirely outside. He
further held that the Board would be dis-
honest, having, to.raise the money for elemen-
tary education, taken from the poor funds
devoted by endowment to the education of
the poor. He moved that the report be re-
ferred back to the Committee.
Mr. Hepworth Dixon seconded the amend-
ment, remarking that the Board were net
arbitrators betiveen the Royal Commissioners
and the Cerporation and manegere of the
other charities.
Mr. Lueraft luta intended to move the pre-
vious question.
Mr. Gover intimated that he weuld not
stand in the way of the motion, and, to faci-
litate it, withdrew his amendment.
Mr. Luoraft went on to show that the
scheme of the Commissioners would plunder
the poor for the benefit of the rich. (" No,
no," and cheers.) The Commissioners pro-
posed to take £lO,OOO from the capital of the
endowment for the erection of two schools in
Westminster, and £15,000 more for a boarding
school within twenty miles of London, and.
£6,000, all to be raised on mortgage, for keep-
ing the schools in repair—was not this plun-
dering the poor? And then they proposed
to charge 102. entrance fee, and school fees,
to be paid in advance, of £2 to £3 in the
lower, and from .£3 t0..£5 in the higher schools
annually—what poor men of the class for
whose benefit the charity was originally en-
dowed could comply with that requirement?
The Commissioners were conscious that their
case was weak, and their object was to bolster
it up with the sanction of the Board, He
suggested that the income of the charity,
(£5,500 a year) should be devoted to scholar-
ships-400 of £lO each, 20 of £25 each, and
10 of £5O each, for the benefit of the parishes
of Westminster and Chelsea.
Mr. Hepworth Dixon seconded the motion
Mr. Pieton supported the original motion
remarking that the circumstances of the
present times were different from those when
these endowments were made, inasmuch as the
education of the poor was provided for by the
State; and he added that the new scheme pro-
vided education to double the number of the
very poor that the previous scheme did.
Mr. H. Cover spoke against the Com-
missioners' scheme, and quoted the resolutions
of the House of Lords to the effect that the
original objects of the endowment should not
be departed from, and that the management
should not be taken out of the hands of the
Corporation.
Canon Barry supported the scheme as
amended by the Committee, as one thoroughly
liberal and calculated to do a valuable work
in the way of secondary education. .

On a division the previous question was
ost by 21 against 7, and the original resoln-
lon was carried. .

Mr. Langdale moved, against the recom-
mendation of the Works Committee, that the
designing of the proposed new offices of the
Board be opened to the competition of four
architects, instead of leaving it to Mr. Robson,
the Board's consulting architect, to prepare
the plans.
Some discussion arose upon this, and
eventually Mr. Langdale's proposition was
carried by 16 against 15 votes.
Some other business, principally of a routine
character, having been transacted, the Board
adjourned.

A large deputation had an interview yester-
day with the Home Secretary, respecting the
long hours cemplaiued of by milliners' and
dressmakers' assistants. A large number of
ladies were present. The Earl of Shaftesbury.
introduced the deputation.
Miss Emily Faithfull read, a, memorial set-
ting forth that women employed •in milliners'
and dressmakers' workrooms are constantly
permitted by the Factory and Workshop Act
of 1871 to work 14
.hours between the hours
of 8 a.m. and 10 p.m. The memorialists.
desired that 10i houts a day (12 hours and
.hours for meats) should be regarded as the
maximum, and that such hours be between
8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; also that on Saturday the
workshops should benlosed at four o!clock.
Mr, Mundella, M.P., pointed out that the Act
compelled the e m ploy ere to work their
employes longer than they would otherwise

do: -
Mr. Powell, M.P., said that the memorialists
would not be satisfied by being told that the
matter was being investigated by inspectors
or even by the Under-Secretary.
Mr. Bruce' engaged in conversation with
several members of the deputation—Mr. W.
H. Smith, Mr. Powell, ,Mr. Mun-della, and
Mr. A.. H. Hill, and in
.course of this the de- '
potation took exception to the power Which
had been given to eertain firms upon appliea"-
tion to work their employes ' fourteen.
hours for eight daya a month for three
months in the year. This order Mr. Bruce con-
tended was limited for One Month, and was
besides purely experimental. He most tell
them, however, that he. had not the' power to
limit the Act of Parliament, but to extend it;
and to 'make any difference the Act dust be.
altered. The modifioation had not been
granted to firms who had not worked the short
hours in the winter.
Mr. Mundella then suggested that a return
should be obtained from the House or Com-
mons showing the number of firms who had
obtained the modification, and what use they
bad made of it, and any further information,
which should be supplied to Mr. Bruin.
Mr. Bruce. said Ito should be only too happy
to receive any -suggestion or information on so
important a matter. .
The deputation then withdrew.

THE. CONDITION OF THE , WORKING

CLASSES.

The annual meeting of the Society for the
Improvement of the Condition of the Work-
ing Classes was held at Willis's Rooms yester-
day, the Earl of Shaftesbury in the chair, The
report showed that the amount received from
all sources during the year vras £5,26,1 12s. 9d.
The expenditure was £5,i36. The houses be-
longing to the society were reported in good
average occupation.
The Right Hon. W. Cowper-Temple, M.P.,
said the condition, moral and physical, of the
labourer depended to a great extent on the
house in which he lived. The condition in
which the labourer existed in the worst parts
of London was such as most seriously to de-
grade his health and morality, as well as that
of his family. And yet an improvement in this i
state of things was n the power of others who
had the welfare of this class at heart. The
demand for the kind of dwellings required
exceeded the supply. There was still a large
floating population seeking dwellings and un-
able to obtain them, being thereby compelled
to press into otherwise crowded dwellings.
The only way to remedy, this was to induce
the sympathy of the wealthier °lasses towards
a movement which had already been pro-
ductive of so much good. He concluded by
moving a resolution in favour of the continued
operations of the society in the same direction.
Sir It. Sterling seconded the motion, which
was carried.
• A vote of thanks was accorded to the chair-
man.
